item.title: The Blizzard Is Here: A Letter to My Future Self
item.description: Amid market turbulence, stay calm and avoid costly mistakes. Learn why panicking during a crash is your worst move—and how to hold firm until recovery.
item.content:encoded:
Read this before you sell.

If you are reading this, the market is crashing. The indices—QQQ, VOO, and everything else—are likely down 30% or more. The news cycle is screaming that the “bubble has popped,” that “this time is different,” and that the economy is heading for a depression. You are likely feeling a physical knot in your stomach, a mix of regret for not selling at the top and fear that your portfolio is going to zero.

Stop. Take a breath. This moment was inevitable. Do not let the panic of the crowd destroy the plan you built in the calm.

Here are the four truths you knew back then, which you must remember now.

1. You Predicted This (The Blizzard Analogy)

Do not act surprised. Remember your own words: “A future drop of more than 30% is virtually certain—like a blizzard in winter.”

You knew this day would come. You knew that equity premiums are not free; they are the reward you get for enduring exactly what you are feeling right now. The market is not “broken.” It is simply winter. You do not burn down your house just because it is snowing outside; you put on a coat and wait for spring.

2. The “Fair-Weather Tourists” Are Leaving. Let Them.

Remember the crowds who bragged about buying QQQ for the AI boom while claiming they “learned nothing” about stocks? They are the ones panicking right now.

  • They bought a narrative, not a business.
  • They borrowed conviction from a rising chart.
  • Now that the chart is falling, their conviction has evaporated.

You are not them. You did not buy these funds because “line goes up.” You bought them as a bet on human innovation and the resilience of the global economy over decades. That thesis has not changed just because the price has. The tourists are selling their assets to you at a discount. Do not join them at the exit.

3. The “Behavior Gap” Is the Real Enemy

The danger right now is not the market; it is you. Statistics (like the DALBAR studies) prove that the average investor destroys their own returns by selling when the pain is highest. They capture 3% while the market returns 10%.

If you sell now, you are crystallizing a temporary decline into a permanent loss. You are volunteering to be part of the statistic that fails. The only way to close the “Behavior Gap” is to endure the volatility that others cannot.

4. The “Zero” Fallacy

Your brain is telling you, “What if it goes to zero?” Let’s be logical. If the S&P 500 or the Nasdaq-100 goes to zero, it means the 100 or 500 largest companies in the world have failed simultaneously. In that scenario, your brokerage account balance won’t matter—you’ll be worrying about food, water, and ammunition.

As long as civilization functions, the market will recover. It always has.

  • It recovered from 1929.
  • It recovered from the 2000 Tech Wreck (even if it took time).
  • It recovered from 2008.

The Command: Sit on Your Hands

Warren Buffett calls investing a “no-called-strike game.” Right now, the market is throwing wild pitches. You do not have to swing. You do not have to “do something” to fix this.

In fact, the hardest and most profitable action you can take right now is absolute inaction.

Turn off the news. Close the brokerage app. Go for a walk. The blizzard is raging, but you have shelter. Wait it out.

Do. Not. Sell.

item.title: My Split Personality in the Stock Market: Why I’m Buffett in a Bull Run and Ready to Quit School in a Crash
item.description: A reminder to myself on how to avoid emotional traps during market swings, focusing on value and probability over fear and greed.
item.content:encoded:
A note to my future self—the one who might be panicking during a crash or getting a big head during a boom.

We often hear the saying, “The stock market is a form of spiritual discipline.” But for most of us, it’s less about Zen and more about a severe case of “investment schizophrenia.”

If you look back at the 2000 Dot-Com Bubble or the 2008 Financial Crisis, countless investors kept repeating the same tired script: They got greedy when they should have been terrified, and terrified when they should have been greedy.

I’m writing this down as a permanent reminder to my future self: When the market starts swinging wildly, don’t fall into the psychological trap that 70% of people do—the endless flip-flop between the “Cocky Gambler” and the “Defeated Student.”

1. 🚨 Watch Out for the “Bull Market Gambler”: When I think “Buffett is Overrated”

When your account balance is constantly in the green and your net worth hits a new high every day, you need to seriously watch out for that “Gambler Persona” whispering in your ear.

The world suddenly looks perfect: everything you buy shoots up, and all the news is fantastic. That’s when a dangerous illusion creeps in: “Maybe I’m actually a genius? Buffett only makes 20% a year, but I pulled 50% this month! Is his old-school stuff even relevant anymore?”

Remember this:

  • That’s the wind, not your wings. Most of your profit in a bull market is $\beta$ (Beta) return, which is just the market rising, or “a rising tide lifting all boats.” You made that 50% because you were standing in the wind tunnel, not because you suddenly grew the ability to fly.
  • Never confuse luck with destiny. The worst thing that can happen to a gambler is winning the first few bets. If you pat yourself on the back for winning a huge, risky bet, you’re just reinforcing a wrong idea in your brain. This “mysterious confidence” will make you bet even bigger next time, until you give back everything you earned, plus your original capital.

A Warning to Myself: The moment you start looking down on conservative, long-term investors, and when you think risk management is for cowards, your mindset has already crashed, even if your account hasn’t. As soon as the tide rolls out, you’ll be the one swimming naked.

2. 🆘 Saving the “Bear Market Student”: When I want to Sell Everything and Swear Off Stocks Forever

When the cycle flips, a black swan lands, and your account drops by 30%, 40%, or even 50%, a different personality takes over—the “Defeated Student Persona.”

Like a student who fails test after test, you’ll fall into a deep state of Learned Helplessness. You’ll start beating yourself up: “I’m so stupid, I got greedy,” “The stock market is a scam,” “I’m done with stocks, I’m taking the rest of my money out and putting it in a savings account.”

This is the exact feeling at the market bottom in 2008. But you must remember: this is the moment that demands the most courage.

  • A loss is a cost, not a sign of incompetence. How can you run a business without buying inventory? A temporary paper loss on a stock is just the “inventory cost” you pay for potential future returns. As long as the logic of the asset you bought hasn’t changed, its value hasn’t changed either.
  • Don’t chop down a tree in the winter. Students fail because they lack ability, but the stock market crashes mostly because of emotional collapse. When others are in peak panic and throwing in the towel (selling at a loss), that’s usually when assets are on the deepest discount.

A Warning to Myself: If your immediate feeling after a huge drop is “shame” and “I need to run away,” instead of “excitement” and “I need to look for gold in the wreckage,” you have completely wasted a crisis. The real transfer of wealth always happens at this exact moment.

3. 🤖 Becoming the Third Person: The Cold, Hard Probability Manager

To survive in this brutal market, I need to kill both the “Gambler” and the “Student” inside me. I must become an Operator.

  • How to Handle a Bull Market: Be extremely humble. Acknowledge the role of luck, and constantly ask: Is my profit based on taking on too much risk? If the market crashed tomorrow, would my investment logic still hold up?
  • How to Handle a Bear Market: Be extremely rational and cold. Strip away all fear and focus only on valuation and probability. If a great company is trading at a 50% discount because of panic, I need to be the buyer, no matter who is selling.

Final Takeaway

Future me, whether you are currently feeling high as a kite looking at your double-bagger account, or sobbing while looking at your position that’s been cut in half, please come back here and read this one last sentence:

Don’t look for validation in good times, and don’t look for defeat in bad times. Be a cold-blooded killer who is accountable only to “value,” and never pays the price for “emotion.”

item.title: Waiting for the wisdom of investment methods and diversified investment
item.description: Exploring the core philosophy of value investing, including the buy-and-hold strategy and the importance of proper diversification, and sharing Berkshire's successful experience.
item.content:encoded:
The Sitting and Waiting Investment Method

If you buy something because its value is undervalued, then when its price rises to your expected level, you must consider selling it. That is difficult. But, if you can buy a few great companies, then you can sit back and relax. That is a good thing. We tend to allocate large sums of money in places where we don’t need to make further decisions.

Diversified Investing

The idea that investment should be as diversified as possible is a crazy notion. We do not believe that highly diversified investments can produce good results. We believe that almost all good investments have relatively low diversification. If you remove our 15 best decisions, our performance would be very mediocre. What you need is not a large amount of action, but extreme patience. You must stick to principles, and when the opportunity comes, you must forcefully grasp it. Over the years, Berkshire has made money by betting on things it is confident about.

item.title: The key to success: patience, learning, and the power of personality
item.description: This article explores the core elements of success, including the importance of patience, the habit of continuous learning, and good personality traits, and cites the wisdom of figures such as Charlie Munger and Benjamin Franklin.
item.content:encoded:
What you need is not a lot of action, but a lot of patience

What you need is not a lot of action, but a lot of patience. You must stick to the principles, and when the opportunity comes, you must grab it with all your might. There are many situations that are worse than being swamped in cash and doing nothing. I remember the time when I lacked cash—I certainly don’t want to go back to that time. ——Charlie Munger

Money is something with extremely powerful reproductive power

This is the stone that can turn all your lead into gold… Remember, money is something with extremely powerful reproductive power. Money gives birth to money, and that money gives birth to even more money. ——Benjamin Franklin

Cultivating Curiosity and the Habit of Continuous Learning

If you want to become smart, the question you must constantly ask is “Why, why, why.” Cultivate yourself into a lifelong learner through extensive reading; cultivate curiosity, and strive to become a little bit smarter every day.

Humility: Acknowledging your ignorance is the beginning of wisdom

  1. Operate only within your clearly defined circle of competence
  2. Identify and verify negative evidence
  3. Resist the desire for false precision and erroneous certainty

Patience: Restraining humanity’s innate preference for action

  1. “Compounding is the eighth wonder of the world” (Einstein), don’t interrupt it unless necessary
  2. Avoid unnecessary transaction taxes and friction costs; never act just for the sake of action
  3. Stay clear-headed when luck comes
  4. Enjoy the results, and enjoy the process, because you are living in the process

The key to success lies in character and learning ability

“Why are some people smarter than others? This has partly to do with innate character. Some people’s characters are not suitable for investing. They are always restless, or always worried. But if you possess a good character—and here, primarily meaning you are very patient and can proactively act when you know you should—then you can gradually understand this game through practice and learning.

Evidently, the wider the sources from which you draw lessons, rather than just from your own bad experiences, the better you will become. I haven’t found anyone who can do this quickly. As an investor, Warren Buffett is much better than when I first met him, and I am the same. If we stagnate at a certain stage, satisfied with the knowledge we already possess, our performance will be much worse than it is now.

So the trick is continuous learning, and I don’t believe that those who don’t enjoy the learning process can continue to learn.”

item.title: Investment equals going out to bet on horses
item.description: You are looking for bets with mispriced odds. That is the essence of investing.
item.content:encoded: “Investing is like horse gambling. We must look for a horse whose probability of winning is one-half, and whose odds are one-to-three. What you are looking for is a wager with mispriced odds. This is the essence of investing. You must possess enough knowledge to know whether the odds of the wager are mispriced. This is value investing.”

item.title: The key to earning big money is not in buying and selling, but in waiting.
item.description: Exploring the philosophy of patience in investing, integrating the investment principles of Jesse Livermore, Charlie Munger, and Warren Buffett, and emphasizing the importance of waiting and long-term holding.
item.content:encoded:
Patience: The Art of Patient Waiting

Look at those hedge funds—do you think they know how to wait? They fundamentally don’t know how to wait! In my personal portfolio, I have held U.S. Treasuries or municipal bonds ranging from $10 million to $12 million for several consecutive years, and then I just stopped touching them, just quietly waiting, waiting…

“As Jesse Livermore said: ‘The secret to making big money is not in buying and selling… but in waiting.’”

Charlie’s Principles and Investment Philosophy

Charlie believes that forethought, patience, self-discipline, and impartiality are the most fundamental guiding principles. No matter how the outside world views things, and no matter how my own emotions fluctuate, he always adheres to these principles. Although many people believe that “one must learn to adapt to random circumstances,” Charlie remains unshaken. If one can firmly adhere to these principles, they can demonstrate one of Munger’s most famous traits: infrequent trading.

Like Buffett, Munger believes that just a few decisions are enough to achieve a successful investment career. Therefore, when Charlie identifies a company he likes, he makes a very large bet, and usually holds the stock of that company for the long term (see “The Investment Performance of Charlie Munger’s Partnership” in Chapter One). Charlie calls this method the “Sit-and-Wait Investment Strategy” (or “Patient Waiting Method”) and clearly points out its advantages: “You pay less in fees to the trader, and you hear less nonsense; if this method works, the tax system will give you an extra 1% to 3% return every year.” In his view, buying just three stocks is enough. Therefore, Charlie is willing to commit a large proportion of capital to individual “watched” opportunities. No Wall Street institution, financial advisor, or open-end fund manager makes such a declaration!

Lessons from Warren’s Investment Course

“When Warren was in business school, he said: ‘I can improve your final financial situation with just one attendance card; this card has 20 slots, so you only have 20 chances to punch in throughout your life—this represents the number of times you can invest in your life. Once you punch the card, you can’t invest anymore. Under this rule, you will truly consider every investment action; you will have to put large sums of money into the projects you truly want to invest in. This way, your performance will be much better.’”

The Rhythm and Strategy of Investing

Quickly eliminate what should not be done, then launch a skilled, interdisciplinary attack on what should be done, and then, when the right opportunity comes—only when the right opportunity comes—act decisively.

item.title: 《Compound Interest Life》 Reading Notes
item.description: Exploring key questions in investment: Is it a one-time capital investment, or phased/gradual investment? Through historical data, market behavior, and psychological analysis, we reveal the core principles of long-term investment.
item.content:encoded:
Should You Invest Lump Sum or Invest Periodically? When you receive an inheritance or another large sum of money, have you ever wondered whether to invest it all at once, or spread the money out and invest it gradually? History over the past 150 years tells us that the North American stock market rises in about two out of every three years. From a statistical perspective, the longer your money stays in the market, the more likely it is to grow. Therefore, the solution to this dilemma is to invest lump sum, while maintaining the awareness that the market could fall at any time. If you are uneasy about investing lump sum, you can set up a simple system for incremental investing (for example, investing 25% of the total amount on the first day of every month, continuing this for four months).

While trillions of dollars are managed by Wall Street professionals who charge high management fees, it is usually the managers who reap massive profits, not the clients.

Don’t think you know more than the market; no one knows more than the market. Don’t act based on your own opinion; you think it’s just your idea, but in reality, millions of people think the same way.

The reason the power of compounding is so counterintuitive is that we rarely view time as an ally. Over time, everything around us seems to degrade and lose value. The top-tier computer bought a few years ago starts slowing down; the house requires expensive maintenance to withstand the elements; even our bodies age. In investing, the situation is exactly the opposite. Investing is one of the few areas where time is on our side.

Investing is frustrating because we always feel we could be doing better. If we invest during a market downturn, we will be disappointed when the market rises sharply because we didn’t invest more. If the market falls after we invest, we will regret it due to bad luck, saying we should have waited longer.

This emotion is widespread, and as investors, we need to recognize it. We can always do better, even if we are right, even if we achieve good returns—we can always do better. Investing is almost certainly going to be disappointing, at least in the short term.

If paying attention to the latest economic developments could make people rich, journalists would already be millionaires. Dear reader, let me tell you a secret: journalists are not millionaires!

News applications aim to draw you into their echo chamber from your phone’s home screen, allowing them to display ads and monitor your behavior. For you, the news is not important information; it is bait that pulls you out of your life and traps you. Turn it off.

In my opinion, the most insidious articles are those that explain why a certain company’s stock rose or fell. These articles are titled things like, “Bank of America Stock Falls Today, Here’s Why,” or “Three Reasons Why Netflix Stock Plunged.” The tone of these articles often makes us think that the author knew the decline was coming and graciously typed out an explanation for us—a small miracle. This makes people even more convinced that predicting a decline is possible. In fact, the authors of these articles don’t know the stock movement; they are merely being “after-the-fact Zhuge Liang” (a reference to a brilliant strategist who often appears after the event), doing so to attract investor clicks.

What smart investors do is forget what might happen and prepare for possibilities through diversification, rational asset allocation, and patience.

In the short term, the stock market is like cocaine—never let it affect you. In most cases, company profits grow over time, and that is the key. What is important is the systematic nature of the investment. Therefore, becoming a good investor requires extreme self-discipline.

In my line of work, the money earned from selling advice is more than the money earned from following it. This is one of the conditions for the magazine industry to survive, the other being the reader’s short memory.

Warren Buffett once said that even if epoch-making disasters like war or pandemics occur, we should not stop investing. In a letter to shareholders, he recounted how his 11-year-old self bought his first batch of stocks on March 11, 1942, three months after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor.

In the three days before Buffett bought his first stock, the headline of The New York Times was “Japanese Forces Break Through Malayan Defenses.” The next day, the paper announced: “Japanese Forces Invade New Guinea from Two Points, Occupy Yangon, and Advance on the Western Front of Burma.” The news on the third day was: “Enemy Artillery Approaches Australia, 98,000 Surrendered in Java, Reportedly.”

Times are always uncertain; violent events constantly threaten world peace, and the risk of economic recession and depression always accompanies us. Here is a brief summary of negative events over the past decade:

  • Russia and Ukraine launched a large-scale conflict, resulting in thousands of deaths.
  • Severe riots occurred at the Capitol Building in Washington D.C.
  • The COVID-19 pandemic caused millions of deaths, leading to a stock market crash and global economic recession.
  • Rebel armed groups attacked oil refineries in Saudi Arabia.

Long-term optimists predict that the world collapses about once every decade.

A stock market crash is like lightning; it can leave even the most rational people stunned. However, just as lightning ushered in the electric age, a stock market crash should be welcomed by most of us.

Many people think they can handle a stock market crash without panicking. But a stock market crash is not just a notification popping up on a phone screen. We calculate our losses in our minds, which might be equivalent to several months or even years of our salary. Only then do we feel genuine panic.

The S&P 500 index averages three drops of 5% or more per year.

Over the past 100 years, the S&P 500 index has experienced a 10% drop approximately every 16 months. Over the last century, a 20% drop occurs on average every seven years. Since the 1950s, the S&P 500 index has also experienced three drops of about 50%, averaging once every 22 years. This famous “market volatility” is so common that we shouldn’t be surprised by it, yet it always surprises us!

The losses caused by downturns are usually temporary. For example, since World War II, the market has averaged only four months to recover from a maximum 20% drop and return to its previous level.

Market returns are never free; they never will be in the future either.

A market adjustment is not a flaw in the financial system. Accepting that investing involves losses is the price you pay for long-term growth. No adjustment, no risk; no risk, no reward.

Setting new highs is the norm, not the exception, in the stock market. Therefore, if you delay investing because the market is strong or at a new high, you might be delaying for a long time!

Since 1928, the S&P 500 index has set a new historical high, on average, every 20 trading days.

From 1926 to 2019, the S&P 500 index rose for nearly three out of every four years. What about the year after a bull market? The index still rises…

After astonishing and absurd surges, such as when the index rises by 50% in 12 months, it should obviously pull back, right? But that’s not the case. Historically, after an incredible year of gains, the market’s return in the second year is indeed negative, with an average return of -1.5%. But after that year of 50% gains, the average market return three years later is 42%, and five years later, it is 66%, not including dividend payments.

If investing were easy, everyone would be rich. Investing shouldn’t be easy; those who think it is easy are fools.

item.title: Stock Market and Economy: Focus on the Owner Rather Than the Dog
item.description: Through vivid metaphors, explain the short-term fluctuations and long-term trends of the stock market, reminding investors to focus on economic fundamentals rather than short-term market changes.
item.content:encoded:
The stock market is like a very excited dog, which is tied to one end of a long leash. The owner holds the leash, and the dog sniffs randomly in all directions. Assuming in this example, the dog owner represents the economy, and he is walking in New York City, starting from the Columbus Circle, passing through Central Park, and arriving at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. From one second to the next, the dog might turn right or left; its movement cannot be precisely predicted.

However, in the long run, the dog’s direction of movement is not mysterious; just like the owner, this dog is moving northeast at a speed of approximately 3 miles per hour.

Surprisingly, almost all people tracking the market are focusing on the dog, rather than the dog owner.

item.title: Never buy things from panting people.
item.description: Explore the investment wisdom of Burton Malkiel and Warren Buffett, emphasizing the importance of avoiding high management fees and overconfidence.
item.content:encoded:
Merton Malkiel’s saying: “Never buy from a panting person.”

Warren Buffett also said something similar: “Be wary of investment activities that make people cheer; true investment genius is usually very boring.”

When trillions of dollars are managed by Wall Street professionals and charge high management fees, it is usually the managers who reap huge profits, not the clients.

Don’t assume you know more than the market; no one knows more than the market. Don’t act based on your own opinions; you think that is your idea alone, but in reality, millions of people think that way."

The lower the annual fee paid by investors, the more money left in their pocket.

item.title: Achieving Financial Independence Through Savings and Investing
item.description: A guide to building wealth through high savings rates and long-term investment strategies in the stock market, avoiding common pitfalls and embracing a resilient approach.
item.content:encoded:
On Saving and Thrifty Lifestyle

The Power of High Savings

  • Save and invest an unwavering 50% of your income.
  • The beauty of a high savings rate is twofold: you learn to live on less, even as you have more to invest.
  • When you can live on 4% of your investments per year, you are financially independent.

Financial Independence vs. Dependence

  • If your lifestyle matches or exceeds your income, you are a slave.
  • It’s better to adapt yourself and your attitudes to the numbers than to adapt the strategies to your psychological comfort levels.

Long-Term Savings Strategy

  • If financial independence is your goal, your savings rate in these years should be high. As you invest that money each month, it serves to smooth out the market’s volatility.
  • Be persistent. Life is uncertain.

On the Stock Market and Investing

Fundamental Investment Rules

  • Rule #1: Never lose money.
  • Rule #2: Never forget rule #1.

The Stock Market as a Wealth-Building Tool

  • The stock market is a powerful wealth-building tool, and you should be investing in it.
  • Embrace indexing.
  • Crashes, pullbacks, and corrections are all absolutely normal.

Avoiding Short-Term Speculation

  • Any investing done short-term is, by definition, speculation.
  • Market timing is an unwinnable game over time. To play this market-timing game well even once, you need to be right twice: first, you need to call the high, and then, you need to call the low.

Market Dynamics and Long-Term Perspective

  • The market always recovers. Always.
  • Everybody makes money when the market is rising. But what determines whether it will make you wealthy or leave you bleeding on the side of the road is what you do during the times it is collapsing.

Common Pitfalls in the Stock Market

  • Most people lose money in the stock market. Here’s why:
    1. We think we can time the market.
    2. We believe we can pick individual stocks.
    3. We believe we can pick winning mutual fund managers.

Dollar-Cost Averaging

  • By dollar-cost averaging, you are betting that the market will drop, saving yourself some pain. For any given year, the odds of this happening are only about 23%. But the market is about 77% more likely to rise, in which case you will have spared yourself some gain. With each new invested portion, you’ll be paying more for your shares.
  • Put all your eggs in one basket and forget about it.

item.title: Realizing the importance of cash again from the stock market crash.
item.description: After Trump announced the latest tariff policy, global stock markets plummeted. This article discusses the common nature of market volatility and why it is crucial to maintain a certain amount of cash within a portfolio.
item.content:encoded:
Trump’s New Tariff Policy and Stock Market Plunge

After Trump announced the latest tariff policy, the global stock market plummeted. So far this year, the market has lost 20%. While I am not panicked, this experience has made me deeply understand one principle: a certain amount of cash must be held in the investment portfolio.

Unexpected Market Events Always Arrive

The market always experiences various unexpected events, once every few years. For example, the 2008 financial crisis, the 2015 market crash, the 2020 Wuhan outbreak, and even the 2025 economic world war. Every market crash is a perfect buying opportunity. The market is filled with cheap assets, and if you don’t have cash, you might miss the chance to get rich.

The Importance of Holding Cash

When the market is running well, the cash in hand can make you feel very uncomfortable, because you are watching the profits slip away from you. However, if you have enough composure, this cash can bring you greater returns in the future. This is the important reason why you must allocate cash in the investment portfolio. Of course, there is also a less important reason: when you need cash, you don’t have to be forced to sell assets.

You might be thinking, why hold cash when the market is good? After all, watching others make money while you are doing nothing—that feeling is indeed unpleasant. But please remember, market volatility is normal, and cash allows you to seize opportunities at critical moments. More importantly, it brings you inner peace and security. 😚

item.title: Three Reasons to Sell Your Stocks
item.description: Explore the key reasons for selling your stocks, including when investment reasons no longer exist, compromised management, and better opportunities. Also, learn about important investment principles to guide your decisions.
item.content:encoded:
There are just three primary reasons for which you should consider selling your stocks:

1. Investment Reasons No Longer Exist

For example, Blockbuster was a great company for many years and was well ahead of the curve when it came to in-home DVD rentals. However, they didn’t adapt to the streaming revolution. In fact, Blockbuster turned down the chance to buy Netflix on three separate occasions.

2. Compromised Management

Small lies eventually lead to bigger lies. If you begin to spot inconsistencies in the way management communicates its shortcomings or if it starts to treat everyone else like a bunch of dunces, it is likely that the management is incompetent. You’re best served by getting out quickly.

3. Better Opportunities

Sometimes, better investment opportunities arise, and it makes sense to reallocate your capital to take advantage of them.

Remember to Keep the Following Investment Principles

  • The Warren Buffett Test: Buy great businesses at fair prices. See if you can describe the business to a 10-year-old.
  • Understand the True Business: How well do you know what drives the profits of the business?
  • Founder Syndrome: How honest and reliable is management? Is there a succession plan in place, or does it all depend on the founder?
  • Intangible Assets: Does the company have any brand loyalty? Does it have intellectual property like patents or trademarks? These are things that don’t show up on a balance sheet.
  • Management Quality: How well does management align the business with the economics of the industry? How well do they reinvest capital?
  • Sales and Marketing: How dedicated is the company to sales and marketing? What is the quality of their teams? How are their key metrics looking year-to-year?
  • Long-Term Focus: Is management focused on short-term metrics, or does it invest resources for the long run?
  • Moat: A moat is a phenomenon that gives a company an unfair advantage in its field. It could be brand loyalty, a superior supply chain, sheer size, etc.
  • Can It Weather a Storm?: How well will the business perform under a stress test?

item.title: The Secret to Successful Investing: Buy and Hold
item.description: Discover the key to successful investing by limiting your activity and focusing on a buy-and-hold strategy. Learn why short-term trading can be risky and how to avoid the temptation to sell your investments too early.
item.content:encoded:
The Secret to Successful Investing

What is the secret to successful investing? It is to do nothing—well, not quite nothing, but our point is that to be successful, you need to limit your activity as much as possible when it comes to managing your investments.

The Risks of Short-Term Trading

Short-term trading involves all kinds of risks. Essentially, a trader is attempting to gauge how the market feels about a stock. Here’s an experiment for you to conduct: walk over to your partner and try to guess how they’re feeling about something. You might be able to guess what is wrong some of the time, but not all the time. This is similar to trying to predict the market’s sentiment.

The Power of Buy and Hold

The most intelligent investment decision you can make is to buy and hold stocks for as long as possible. Leave the constant jumping in and out to the traders and other speculators. Resist everything that can potentially cause you to exit early or trade too much in a single stock.

If you don’t have the cash to pay your bills, you’re going to be tempted to sell some of your investments before they have a chance to blossom fully.

Essential Savings Priorities

  1. Your Rainy Day Fund: 3-6 months’ worth of living expenses that you’ve saved up in case you or your partner lose your jobs.
  2. Readily Accessible Cash: This money should not be invested under any circumstances. Your rainy day fund should be held in readily accessible cash.
  3. Tuition Payments: Money that is needed to pay bills or your child’s tuition should not be invested in the markets.
  4. Down Payments: Even if you’re planning on purchasing a home several years down the road, don’t rely on the stock market to generate enough money for a down payment.

item.title: Money that should never be used for investment
item.description: Learn how to properly manage your financial safety nets, including rainy day funds, tuition payments, and down payments, by keeping them in safe, liquid, and readily accessible forms.
item.content:encoded:
If you don’t have the cash to pay your bills, you may be tempted to sell some of your investments before they have a chance to fully blossom.

Your Rainy Day Fund

  • Purpose: A 3-6 month reserve of living expenses in case you or your partner lose your jobs.
  • Storage: This money should be held in readily accessible cash and not invested under any circumstances.

Tuition Payments

  • Purpose: Money needed to pay bills or your child’s tuition.
  • Guidance: This money should not be invested in the markets. Ensure it is kept in a safe, liquid form.

Down Payments

  • Purpose: Funds for a future home purchase.
  • Guidance: Even if you’re planning on purchasing a home several years down the road, avoid relying on the stock market to generate enough money for a down payment. Keep these funds in a stable, low-risk account.

item.title: Pre-Trading Checklist *(Alternative: Stock Market Operation Checklist)*
item.description: This article provides a detailed pre-trading checklist for the stock market, covering key steps such as buying, selling, and rebalancing. It helps investors reduce emotional bias through a systematic process, avoid common mistakes, and achieve long-term, stable investment returns.
item.content:encoded:
Stock Market Trading Pre-Checklist

I. General Principles (Must Read Before Every Trade)

  1. Goal Confirmation

    • Does my trade serve my long-term investment goals?
    • Am I trading impulsively due to short-term market fluctuations, emotions, or external advice? (If “Yes,” pause and calmly review the situation)

  2. Cost Awareness

    • Do transaction fees (commission, stamp duty, management fees) significantly impact the return?
    • Is “friction cost” accumulating due to frequent trading?

  3. Discipline

    • Does the trade adhere to the pre-set strategy (e.g., DCA plan, rebalancing rules)?
    • Is there a “regret mindset” (e.g., annoyance over not acting in time)?

II. ETF Purchase Pre-Checklist

1. Basic Conditions

  • Is the long-term holding period ≥ 3-5 years? (Conflicts with the concept of short-term trading vs. passive investment)
  • Is the tracked index clear (e.g., S&P 500, CSI 300) and sufficiently liquid? (Avoid niche or complex derivatives)
  • Are the fee rates reasonable (e.g., annual fee ≤ 0.3%)? (Low cost is a core advantage of passive investment)

2. Market and Valuation

  • Is the current market in a state of extreme overvaluation? (Refer to PE/PB quantiles: Caution is needed if the S&P 500 PE is above the 25th percentile)
  • Am I blindly following the trend due to recent gains? (Beware of the “this time is different” cognitive trap)

3. Risk Management

  • Is the portfolio overly concentrated in a single industry or region? (e.g., Tech stocks exceeding 40%, requiring diversification)
  • Have I reserved enough cash to handle Black Swan events? (e.g., If emergency reserves are insufficient, postpone adding more)

4. Emotional Test

  • Is the reason for buying based on rational analysis, rather than “Fear of Missing Out” (FOMO)?
  • Am I buying at a low price due to panic selling? (When the market crashes, assess calmly, don’t just blindly buy)

III. ETF Sale Pre-Checklist

1. Core Principles

  • Is there a clear, non-negotiable reason to sell? (Passive investment prioritizes “holding”; selling must be deliberate)
  • Am I selling in a panic due to short-term volatility (e.g., 20% drawdown within 1 year)? (Historical data shows short-term drawdowns usually recover)

2. Necessity Assessment

  • Has the index component significantly deviated from the target (e.g., one company in a Tech ETF has excessive weight)?
  • Has the goal been achieved (e.g., the education fund has accumulated the required capital)?

3. Risk and Alternatives

  • Does the capital have a clear destination with higher potential returns after selling? (e.g., shifting to bonds or cash, requiring opportunity cost assessment)
  • Am I “cutting losses and exiting” due to a market crash? (Historical experience shows exiting at a low point often misses the recovery)

4. Emotion and Discipline

  • Am I trading based on media-driven panic sentiment? (e.g., “Doomsday” or “Bull Market End” narratives require calm verification)
  • Have I violated the pre-set selling rules (e.g., take-profit line or stop-loss line)? (Undisciplined selling easily undermines the long-term strategy)

IV. Rebalancing Operation Checklist

1. Trigger Conditions

  • Has the preset time interval been reached (e.g., quarterly/annually)? (To avoid excessive adjustments)
  • Has the asset allocation deviated from the target ratio by more than ±5%-10%? (e.g., Stock allocation should be 60%, but is currently 70%)

2. Cost and Efficiency

  • Will the rebalancing lead to high costs (e.g., frequent trading fees, taxes)?
  • Am I prioritizing using new capital for adjustment rather than selling existing holdings? (e.g., using new funds to top up under-allocated assets during DCA)

3. Market Judgment

  • Am I adjusting due to extreme market valuation (e.g., Tech stocks are overvalued, shifting to value stocks)? (Requires caution to avoid the “market timing selection” trap)
  • Am I adjusting the strategic allocation due to long-term trend changes (e.g., energy transition)? (Requires combining fundamental research, not just short-term volatility)

4. Discipline

  • Does the operation align with the “Buy Low, Sell High” logic of rebalancing? (e.g., selling over-allocated assets when they are overvalued, and buying under-allocated assets when they are undervalued)

V. Post-Operation Record (Mandatory After Every Execution)

  1. Operation Type: Buy / Sell / Rebalance
  2. Decision Basis: List the key points marked “Yes” in the checklist
  3. Market Environment: Current PE/PB, Interest Rates, Economic Cycle Stage
  4. Emotional Score: 1-10 (1 = Extreme Panic, 10 = Extreme Greed)
  5. Review Marker: Record the outcome after 3 months and confirm if it met expectations

VI. Ultimate Question (Muttered Before Every Trade)

“In 10 years, will this decision make me richer or will it make me regret it more?” “If I couldn’t trade for the next year, would my current operation still be rational?” If a trade cannot withstand the test of a year-long pause, it is highly likely to harm long-term returns.

By following this systematic process, you can reduce emotional interference and avoid common mistakes (such as chasing highs and selling lows, or over-trading), ultimately achieving stable compound growth through a passive investment strategy. Wishing you successful investing!

item.title: Why should you absolutely avoid short-term trading?
item.description: This paper explores the randomness of market sentiment, the temptation of short-term trading, and the importance of avoiding emotional interference in investment decisions, emphasizing the necessity of establishing a rational decision-making mechanism.
item.content:encoded:
Ultimately, it still comes down to that famous saying: The market is a voting machine in the short term, and a weighing machine in the long term.

Speculation is a 0 and a Game - My Lessons in Speculation

The Essence of Reducing Trading Frequency

Investment vs. Speculation in “Enough”

Market Sentiment is Random

The market is essentially like a person of average intelligence. You might occasionally guess the market’s sentiment, but to make money, you need to guess correctly twice (the buying point + the selling point). And if you guess wrong just once, you will lose money. This is a very simple mathematical problem.

Some Forces Want You to Trade Short-Term

There are always stories that make you want to trade short-term for quick money. This is similar to seeing news about a major jackpot—it is essentially an advertisement. This is because securities companies, exchanges, and tax bureaus all like you to trade frequently and repeatedly. They are leveraging the greed in your nature to entice you into these speculative operations.

Never Make Investment Decisions During Strong Emotions

Never make investment decisions when you are experiencing strong emotions. Whether that emotion is fear, excitement, sadness, or greed and impulse, they act like a fog obscuring rational judgment.

  • When the market crashes sharply, the fear fueled by adrenaline might cause you to sell quality assets at a bargain price;
  • When the bull market is rampant, the euphoria driven by dopamine easily tempts you to buy at high prices. Even sudden sad events in life can act like an invisible filter, distorting your perception of the risk-reward ratio. True investment wisdom lies in establishing a decision-making mechanism that is insulated from emotional fluctuations—replacing ad-hoc judgment with pre-set trading discipline, and hedging against human weaknesses with data-supported valuation models.

Pre-Checklist for Stock Market Operations

item.title: Rebalancing between aggressive and defensive stocks
item.description: Rebalancing is an investment strategy that manages risk and optimizes returns by adjusting asset allocation. It is suitable for choppy or sector rotation markets, but attention must be paid to the impact of transaction costs and market trends.
item.content:encoded:
1. Basic Concepts of Rebalancing

  • Asset Allocation: Investors set the proportion of different asset classes (e.g., stocks, bonds, cash) based on their risk tolerance and return goals.
  • Market Fluctuation: Market fluctuations can cause asset proportions to deviate from the target (e.g., a rise in stocks might make their share in the portfolio too high).
  • Rebalancing: Adjusting the portfolio back to the target proportion by buying and selling assets.

2. Methods of Rebalancing

  • Time-based Rebalancing: Adjusting the portfolio at fixed time intervals (e.g., quarterly or annually).
  • Ratio-based Rebalancing: Adjusting when a specific asset class deviates from the target proportion by more than a certain threshold (e.g., 5%).

3. Advantages of Rebalancing

  • Risk Control: Prevents a single asset from having too high a proportion, thereby reducing risk.
  • Discipline: Avoids emotional trading, maintaining the stability of the investment strategy.
  • Return Optimization: May enhance long-term returns by buying low and selling high.

4. Disadvantages of Rebalancing

  • Transaction Costs: Frequent adjustments may increase trading fees.
  • Tax Implications: In taxable accounts, rebalancing may generate capital gains tax.
  • Market Trends: In a unidirectional market (trend), rebalancing may reduce returns.

5. Implementation of Rebalancing

  • Determine Target Proportion: Setting asset allocation based on risk preference.
  • Monitor Portfolio: Regularly checking asset proportions.
  • Execute Adjustment: Restoring the target proportion by buying and selling assets.

Summary

Rebalancing is a tool for “exchanging short-term transaction costs for long-term risk control.” It is suitable for volatile or sector-rotating markets, but may incur opportunity costs in unidirectional trend markets. When executing, it is recommended to combine threshold rules (e.g., rebalancing after a 10% deviation) rather than mechanically operating based on time. Furthermore, it is recommended to operate a maximum of twice a year.

item.title: The timing of the investor's shift from offense to defense (or defensive to offensive)
item.description: This paper explores offensive and defensive strategies in investment, pointing out that aggressive strategies may yield high returns but come with high risk, while defensive strategies focus on asset safety and risk control, emphasizing the importance of making trade-offs based on personal goals and market conditions.
item.content:encoded:
To Be a Winner, or to Avoid Being a Loser?

  1. Being proactive can yield greater rewards, but in the long run, it is not always beneficial.
  2. When luck is bad, you may encounter developments that are less than expected, leading to frustration.
  3. Short-term success is generally recognized, but there is insufficient attention paid to its persistence and stability in the records.

Timing of Offensive and Defensive Shifts

Few people (if any) have the ability to instantly adjust tactics to match market conditions, so investors should stick to one method, hoping that this method can apply to various different situations.

They might adopt an aggressive strategy, hoping to earn a lot when investments succeed and recoup costs when they fail; or they might emphasize a defensive strategy, hoping to match market performance during a bull market and lose less than others during a bear market.

We cannot determine the exact timing for offense and defense So, we can only choose based on our own conditions. The safety of your asset portfolio should be determined by how much potential return you are willing to sacrifice. There is no correct answer, only a trade-off.

Offense

An aggressive tactic raises potential highs and lowers potential lows. However, if you exclusively use an offensive investment approach, when things go wrong, it might prevent you from recovering. On the other hand, defensive investment can help you navigate difficult periods, giving you enough time to enjoy the ultimate returns brought by smart investing.

Defense

  1. Defensive investment has two main elements. The first is eliminating underperforming assets from the portfolio. To achieve this, the best approach is to conduct in-depth evaluations, adopt high stock selection standards, demand low prices, and set a relatively large margin of error (which will be mentioned later in this chapter). Furthermore, do not bet on uncertain scenarios such as continuous bullish trends or beautiful forecasts and developments.

  2. The second element is avoiding market bear markets, especially avoiding the risk of an imminent crash. In addition to excluding individual underperforming assets from the portfolio (as mentioned earlier), defensive investment also requires thoughtful asset diversification, limiting overall risk exposure, and focusing on safety.

item.title: Taking an uncertain world as the investment premise
item.description: This paper discusses that when investing, one should focus on knowable industry and company value, rather than unpredictable macroeconomics, and emphasizes addressing uncertainty through defensive strategies, contrarian operations, and a skeptical attitude, ensuring survival and success in unfavorable markets.
item.content:encoded:
1. We should spend time trying to find value in knowable factors such as industries, companies, and securities, rather than making decisions based on our predictions about the relatively unknowable overall economic world and market trends.
  2. Because we cannot know the exact shape of the future, we must acquire value through methods such as firm conviction, views derived from future analysis, and buying in at a lower price when opportunities arise.
  3. We must adopt defensive investing because many outcomes may be unfavorable to us. More importantly, we must confirm the ability to survive in the market under negative outcomes, rather than guaranteeing maximum returns under favorable outcomes.
  4. To increase the chances of success, when extreme situations occur, we must emphasize that the actions taken should be contrary to the crowd: being aggressive when the market is sluggish, and being cautious when the market is euphoric.
  5. Because the results are inherently highly uncertain, unless they have been verified through many experiments, we must view the decisions and the resulting outcomes with a skeptical perspective—whether they are good outcomes or bad outcomes.

item.title: Money is transferred from impatient people to patient people.
item.description: This paper explores the importance of patience in wealth accumulation, pointing out that while speculation may bring short-term gains, true success stems from sustainable compound growth.
item.content:encoded:
“You don’t need massive actions, you need massive patience. Money transfers from the pockets of the impatient to the pockets of the patient.”

Speculation, once or twice, might allow you to earn massive profits, but in the long run, it is irreplicable, unsustainable, and even destined to fail. True success relies on compound interest, relies on daily progress (small, consistent steps), and relies on sustainable development.

item.title: Buy low, sell high
item.description: In investing, contrarian trading requires courage but can bring substantial returns. Mastering extreme market opportunities is a strategy that every investor should prioritize.
item.content:encoded:
When buying when others are depressed and selling when others are excited, it all requires the greatest courage, but it also provides the most generous profits.

“Buy low and sell high” is an ancient saying, but investors who are lost in the market cycle often do the opposite. The appropriate action should be to take contrarian behavior:

  1. Buy when the crowd dislikes, and sell when the crowd likes.
  2. Market extremes of “only once in a lifetime” seem to occur roughly every decade. The frequency is not so high that investors can make a living from it, but for any investor, trying to do so should be an important part of their trading strategy.

item.title: The negative impact of confronting emotions
item.description: This paper explores seven mindsets that lead to erroneous investment decisions, including greed, fear, self-deception, herd mentality, jealousy, overconfidence, and the capitulation mindset. It reveals how these psychological factors universally affect investors and trigger frequent and repetitive behavioral errors.
item.content:encoded:
The desire to earn more, the fear of missing out on opportunities, the personality trait of comparing oneself to others, the influence of the group, and the dream of successful investment—these factors are almost universally present. Consequently, they exert a profound collective influence on most investors and the market, resulting in errors. These errors are frequent, widespread, and tend to repeat themselves.

Seven Mindsets Leading to Errors in Decision-Making

Many people possess the intelligence to analyze data, but few are able to observe things deeply and withstand the powerful influence of psychological factors. In other words, many people arrive at similar conclusions based on their own analysis and cognition, but they act in drastically different ways due to varying psychological influences. The biggest investment bias does not come from information or analysis, but from mindset.

Greed

Greed is defined as “an excessive or exhaustive desire, and usually a reprehensible possessiveness, especially for wealth or profit.”

Greed is an extremely powerful force. Its power is so great that it can override common sense, risk aversion, caution, logic, the memory of past painful lessons, determination, panic, and other elements that would normally make an investor avoid trouble. Furthermore, greed occasionally leads investors to join the pursuit of profit, only to pay the price in the end.

Fear

Fear, like greed, implies excess. Therefore, fear is more akin to panic. Fear is an excessive worry that causes investors to remain inactive when they should be taking positive action.

Self-Deception

Nothing is easier to self-deceive than oneself, because everyone, as long as they wish to, will believe it is true. Investors are always looking for a panacea, calling it the “Holy Grail” or the “Free Lunch,” but everyone wants a ticket that turns them into a wealthy person without taking any risks. Few question whether this ticket exists, or why they should receive it. Most importantly, the average person always maintains hope.

What factors make people believe in a panacea?

  1. First, there is usually a factual basis for it.
  2. Then, a set of seemingly intelligent theories is fabricated, which the believers promote everywhere to persuade others. Subsequently, this theory accidentally generates profits, either because the theory has some value or simply because new believers join and drive up the price of the target asset. Finally, it appears to be a definite way to acquire wealth, and this creates a craze.

Herd Mentality (Conformity)

Not even when one insists on their own opinion, even if the crowd’s view is clearly absurd. Time and time again, the pressure of the herd and the desire to get rich cause people to abandon independent judgment and skepticism, suppressing their innate risk-averse mindset to believe in the unreasonable. Since this situation occurs so regularly, something must be at work, rather than merely random influence.

Envy

Even if the force of greed is negative, it at least motivates others to strive for more profit. But the negative influence of comparing oneself to others is even stronger. This is what we consider the most dangerous trait of human nature.

A person who might be happy when isolated can feel miserable when they see others doing better. In the investment world, you will find that most investors find it difficult to sit idly by and watch others earn more money than them.

Hubris (Overconfidence)

It is an enormous challenge to remain objective and prudent when facing the following realities:

  1. We evaluate and compare short-term investment performance.
  2. During a bull market, making an inappropriate, even reckless, decision to increase risk often yields the best returns (and most of the time, it is a bull market).
  3. The best returns bring the greatest reward. When things go right, feeling smart and having others agree with it is a very pleasant feeling.

In contrast, a thoughtful investor works diligently, earning stable returns during a bull market and losing less than others during a bear market. They avoid high-risk behavior because they know there is much they do not understand, and they suppress their hubris. In my view, this is the best formula for long-term wealth creation, but it does not satisfy the mindset in the short term. Emphasizing humility, caution, and risk control is not a glamorous path, and of course, investment should not seek glamour, but that is what people often think.

Surrender Mentality

This is an investment behavior that is consistently observed in the later stages of a cycle. Investors try their best to stick to their beliefs, but when they cannot resist economic or psychological pressure, they surrender and follow the trend. Often, asset prices are too high and continue to rise, or the price is too low and continues to fall. Eventually, these trends shake the investor’s mindset, beliefs, and determination. Others profit because you refuse to buy a stock, while the stock you choose to buy hovers at a low price every day. Furthermore, the investment concept you originally thought was unsafe and unwise seems to be going in the right direction—selling the overpriced stock and buying the underpriced stock—but the investor does not do it. The tendency toward self-doubt, mixed with news of others’ success, forms a powerful force that leads the investor to make the wrong decision. And when this trend continues for a longer period, the force becomes stronger—this is another influence factor we must fight against.

item.title: The higher the risk, the greater the uncertainty of return.
item.description: This paper provides an in-depth exploration of the myth linking high-risk investment and high returns, highlighting that high risk does not guarantee high rewards, and analyzing the cognitive blind spots humans possess when facing risk, as well as the true nature of market operations.
item.content:encoded:
Especially during a bull market, you often hear many people say: “High-risk investments bring higher returns. If you want to make more money, you must take on higher risks.” In fact, it is not possible to generate high returns solely through high-risk investments. Why? The answer is simple: If high-risk investments could reliably create high returns, then their risk wouldn’t be high!

The correct way to put it is that, in order to attract capital, high-risk investments must offer higher potential returns, higher guaranteed returns, or higher expected returns, but this absolutely does not mean that the higher potential return will always be realized.

  1. Risk only exists in the future, and we cannot know exactly what the future will hold… When we look back at the past, the facts are clearly evident—we know that something happened. However, this certainty does not mean that the process that produced the result was clear and reliable. In every past situation, many things could have happened. But because only one thing happened, we tend to underestimate the existence of variability.
  2. When deciding whether or not to take on risk, I first assume that the normal situation will repeat itself. Although the normal situation does indeed repeat itself most of the time, sometimes something very different happens… Occasionally, rare things happen.
  3. Our predictions usually revolve around historical norms, at most making small adjustments… The key point is that most people typically predict the future will be similar to the past, and they underestimate the possibility of change.
  4. We have heard many predictions about the “worst-case scenario,” but the results are often even worse. Let me tell you about my father’s story. He was a habitual gambler, and one day he heard about a horse race with only one horse running, so he bet his rent money. However, halfway through the race, the horse jumped the rail and ran away. Things always tend to become worse than the average person expects. Perhaps “worst-case scenario” means “the worst case we have seen so far,” but it doesn’t mean it is the worst case of the future. The situation in 2007 was far worse than many people assumed for the worst-case scenario.
  5. Risk changes. If we say there is a “2% mortgage default rate” every year, even if the average figure over many years is indeed that, there is still a possibility that an abnormal amount of defaults will occur at some point, dragging down the performance of structured financial products. Some investors, especially those using high leverage, cannot get through this difficult time.
  6. People tend to overestimate their ability to measure risk, and they also overestimate their understanding of investment mechanisms they have never seen before. Theoretically, what makes humans different from other species is that we can point out something is dangerous without personally experiencing it. We don’t need to burn ourselves to know not to sit on the stove. However, during a bull market, this mechanism often fails to operate. People don’t first understand the risk; instead, they tend to overestimate their ability to understand new financial products.
  7. Finally, and most importantly, most people believe that taking on risk is the main way to make money, and enduring high risk usually brings high rewards. The market must be arranged to make it seem like this, otherwise, people wouldn’t participate in high-risk investments. But the market won’t operate this way forever, otherwise, high-risk investments wouldn’t be high-risk. It is only when taking on risk does not bring the desired result that we realize this investment method truly doesn’t work, and we remember what risk actually is.

item.title: Investing is a competition of public sentiment (or: a race for popularity), and the most dangerous thing is buying when the hype is at its peak.
item.description: This paper explores how the behavior of forced sellers and buyers influences investment opportunities under extreme market conditions, and analyzes the inverse relationship between perceived risk and actual risk, reminding investors to maintain caution and rationality during bubbles and crashes.
item.content:encoded:
It is best to acquire stocks when they are collapsing, especially those that are forced to sell regardless of the price. There is nothing better than this; many of our best trades are made for this very reason. However, we have two observations: You cannot rely solely on buying stocks from forced sellers or selling stocks to forced buyers to make a living, as they won’t always appear in the market—they only emerge during extreme crises and rare bubbles. In our world, buying stocks from forced sellers is the best thing, so the worst thing is becoming a forced seller. This means it is crucial to arrange your finances well; you must ensure that you can hold stocks even in the most difficult times without being forced to sell. This requires both long-term capital and strong psychological fortitude.

During a bubble, investors’ obsession with market momentum will override any concept of value or fair price. Greed (coupled with the internal pain of watching others easily profit) will eliminate the necessary caution.

“Universal Belief in No Risk” is a Rare High Risk

In a bull market, especially after the rally has continued for a period, investors often say: “Risk is my friend, because the more risk I take, the higher the reward will be, so please give me more risk.” The reality is that risk tolerance is completely opposite to successful investing. When investors are not afraid of risk, they accept it without demanding compensation… and the compensation for that risk disappears.

A Major Factor in Risk Arises from Believing Risk is Low

“No matter what price, I won’t buy it; everyone knows this risk is too high.” I hear many such statements in life, and I have participated in the best investment opportunities because of them…

I firmly believe that investment risk most often occurs where it is least noticed, and vice versa:

When everyone believes that something is high risk, their willingness to buy usually drives the price down to a low-risk level. Universal pessimism makes it the lowest-risk thing because all the optimistic factors in the price have been eliminated. Of course, as the experience of the “Pretty Fifty” investors proves, when everyone believes that something has no risk, the price is driven up to a highly risky level. No risk means there is nothing to fear, and therefore, no reward is provided or demanded for taking that risk—meaning there is no “risk premium.” This turns the most lauded thing into the riskiest thing.

item.title: Even if the market denies it, you must bravely persist.
item.description: This paper explores investors' psychological reactions during market price volatility, and explains why buying during a price decline may be crucial for profitability. The article also emphasizes the importance of having a strong conviction regarding intrinsic value.
item.content:encoded:
We learned in our introductory course on microeconomics that the demand curve slopes downward to the right: as the price increases, the quantity demanded decreases. In other words, when prices are high, the quantity demanded is relatively low, and when prices are low, the quantity demanded is relatively high. This makes perfect sense, which is why stores perform better when they have special offers. While this operates in many places, it is far from the case in the investment world. Here, many people prefer to buy assets when prices are rising because they feel it confirms their decision; but when prices fall, they are less inclined to buy assets because they start to doubt their initial purchase decision.

No one can comfortably face a loss. Eventually, everyone will wonder: “Maybe I am wrong, the market is right.” The most dangerous time is when they start speculating: “It has fallen too much; I better get rid of it before the stock becomes wallpaper.” This is the mindset that leads to a stock bottoming out… and triggers a frenzy of selling pressure.

In a declining market, there are two basic elements for making a profit: you must have your own view on the intrinsic value, and you must be steadfast. Even if the falling price suggests you are wrong, you must be brave enough to buy. Oh, right, there is a third element: your view must be correct.

item.title: Accurately estimate substantive value
item.description: For value investors, “asset” is not merely a concept of short-term investment because it is attractive (or because others find it attractive). An asset is a tangible object that should have clear intrinsic value. If it can be bought at a price lower than its intrinsic value, it should be considered for purchase. Therefore, smart investing should be based on the estimation of intrinsic value, and these estimations must be calculated rigorously using available information. (Qiao) 〈The Most Important Thing〉 (THE MOST IMPORTANT THING)
item.content:encoded: For value investors, “asset” is not merely a concept of short-term investment because it is attractive (or because others find it attractive). An asset is a tangible object that should have clear intrinsic value. If it can be bought at a price lower than its intrinsic value, it should be considered for purchase. Therefore, smart investing should be based on the estimation of intrinsic value, and these estimations must be calculated rigorously using available information. (Qiao) 〈The Most Important Thing〉 (THE MOST IMPORTANT THING)

item.title: Efficient Market and Inefficient Market
item.description: Explore the assumptions behind Efficient Market Theory, its limitations in the real world, and how to balance the perspectives of efficiency and inefficiency in investment.
item.content:encoded:
Assumptions Behind Efficient Market Theory

  1. There are many investors who put in effort to research.
  2. They are smart, diligent, objective, active, and well-prepared.
  3. They can access available information, and their access channels are generally the same.
  4. They can buy, sell, or short (i.e., bet on a decline) all assets.

Because of these reasons, the Efficient Market Hypothesis posits that available information is smoothly and effectively integrated into prices, adjusting when prices do not match value, thereby eliminating the discrepancy.

Certain Assets Conform to the Efficient Market, and the Main Types Are

  • Assets that are widely known and tracked by many people;
  • Assets that are socially accepted, non-controversial, or not taboo;
  • Assets that have clear and easy-to-understand advantages, at least superficially;
  • Information related to the asset type and its components is disseminated universally and fairly.

Issues in the Above Assumptions

Most people are driven by greed, fear, jealousy, or other emotions, which disrupt the possibility of objectivity, allowing obvious errors to take advantage of the situation.

Consider These Questions

  • When thousands of investors rush to buy, willing to drive up the price of cheap assets, why are there still cheap assets?
  • When the return relative to the risk is clearly high, does that mean you might be ignoring some hidden risks?
  • Why are sellers willing to accept a price that allows you to gain excess returns when selling an asset?
  • Do you really know more information about the asset than the seller?
  • If this is such a good deal, why isn’t anyone else rushing to buy it?

There is one more thing to remember: The market being efficient today does not mean it will be efficient forever.

Conclusion

No market is perfectly efficient or perfectly inefficient; it is merely a matter of degree. I sincerely appreciate the opportunities provided by inefficient markets, but I also respect the concept of efficient markets, and I firmly believe that the mainstream securities market has enough efficiency that trying to find a winner within it is basically a waste of time.

There is a fish in every pond; if you play for forty-five minutes and still don’t know who that fish is, then you are that fish.

item.title: Second-Level Thinking
item.description: This article explores the "second-layer thinking," which is crucial in investment, explaining how to exceed the market average return through deep analysis and unique perspectives, and highlights that successful investing requires not just simple logical judgment, but a comprehensive understanding of complex market dynamics.
item.content:encoded:
Investment Thinking Must Be Different

The exceptional insights, intuition, value concepts, and understanding of market psychology required to maintain returns above average. To achieve this, you need second-level thinking.

Doing the right thing might be a necessary condition for successful investing, but it is not a sufficient condition. You must do more things right than others, which means your way of thinking must be different.

What is Second-Level Thinking?

  1. First-level thinking says: “This is a good company, so buy this stock!” Second-level thinking says: “This is a good company, but everyone thinks this company is good, so it isn’t a good company. This stock is overvalued, the market price is too high, so sell!”
  2. First-level thinking says: “From a forward-looking perspective, economic growth is sluggish and inflation is rising, so sell the holdings!” Second-level thinking says: “The economic outlook is terrible, but everyone is selling stocks out of panic, so you should buy!”
  3. First-level thinking says: “I believe this company’s earnings will decline, so sell!” Second-level thinking says: “I believe the decline in this company’s earnings will be less than expected; an unexpected surprise will boost the stock price, so buy!”

People Who Practice Second-Level Thinking Consider Many Things

  • What range of outcomes might occur in the future?
  • Which outcome do I believe will occur?
  • How high is the probability that my view is correct?
  • What is the market consensus?
  • How large is the difference between my expectation and the market consensus?
  • How closely does the market price of this asset align with the price believed by the market consensus?
  • And what about my own price?
  • Is the consensus sentiment reflected in the price overly optimistic or pessimistic?
  • If the market consensus proves to be correct, what effect will that have on the asset price?
  • If my expectation is the correct one, what effect will that have?

There is a clear and significant difference in the workload between first-level thinking and second-level thinking. The number of people capable of second-level thinking is obviously much smaller than those capable of first-level thinking. First-level thinkers look for simple formulas and easy answers. Second-level thinkers know that successful investing is contrary to simplicity. This doesn’t mean you won’t encounter many people who try to make investing sound simple, I call them “mercenaries.” Securities companies want you to believe that everyone is capable of investing, and that every transaction only costs ten dollars. Fund companies don’t want you to believe that you are capable of investing, but they want you to believe that they are capable of investing, so you will put your money into actively managed funds and pay higher management fees.

item.title: 《Financial Freedom Notes》
item.description: This article explores the true value and strategies of stock market investing, emphasizing the importance of seeking opportunities during market downturns, maintaining rationality, and properly allocating assets, while also revealing common psychological biases and behavioral pitfalls of investors.
item.content:encoded:
When the market is most valuable, it is when no one wants to buy stocks, rather than when the auntie sweeping the floor next to you can tell you exactly how high a certain stock will rise. History’s repeated cycles of bull and bear markets tell us that when everyone in the market is avoiding purchasing these assets, it is often when stock prices are at their lowest. If you look at things from a long-term perspective, market downturns are precisely the opportunity for value investors to select good stocks. Therefore, you must know how to exit when the crowds are roaring, and enter when it is dark—that is true high selling and low buying.

Most financial planners do not truly care about your interests, no matter how friendly and kind they appear to be to you on the surface.

To stay financially safe from risk, we must accumulate assets, not liabilities. The safest way to ensure lifelong use is to spend less and earn more, and then invest the remaining money rationally.

No matter how high a person’s salary is, if they cannot still live comfortably and pleasantly when they lose their job, it only proves that they are not truly wealthy.

At a minimum, they should meet the following two standards to be considered “wealthy”:

  • They can choose not to work and do not have to worry about making a living.
  • Their held investments, pensions, or trusts can guarantee returns that are twice the average income of a middle-income family in the country for life.

In the pursuit of wealth and achieving financial independence, many people make a foolish mistake: they like to create the illusion that they look rich, rather than becoming truly rich.

The best way to achieve diversification in a stock investment portfolio is to find a low-fee index fund.

They fundamentally cannot beat the market; that simply will not happen.

Kahneman discovered through research that human instinctive behavior negatively affects investment decisions, and he received the Nobel Prize precisely for this research. He believes that many people feel that if you give excellent fund managers enough time, they will be able to beat the market index.

You know to rush to buy when stores are on sale, so why don’t you buy when stocks are at “jump-off-the-building” prices?

Stock investing inevitably requires some luck, but in the long run, good luck and bad luck will offset each other. To achieve sustained success, you must rely on skill and good principles.

Maintaining rationality secures an average return of 10%.

The stock market is like a manic dog; you never know where it will run.

The simplest way to build a rational, diversified investment account is to utilize stock and bond index funds.

However, when the stock market enters an accelerated upward phase, everyone becomes ecstatic and captivated by the profits brought by rising stock prices. At this time, most people disregard their bonds (if they hold them), buying more stocks with all their might. Even many financial advisors become victims of this temptation. But this practice of setting aside the predetermined stock-to-bond allocation is precisely paving the road to disaster for themselves.

When you hold a stock market index fund, you actually possess something as real and reliable as the ground beneath your feet.

When manic investors meet manic stocks, a bubble will appear.

Those who ignore the “Bible of the stock market”—the idea that “profit growth is directly related to stock price growth”—will ultimately lose everything.

The stock market after the “9/11” event is exactly opposite to the stock market at the end of the 1990s. Although stock prices plummeted like soccer-ball sized hail, corporate profits were hardly affected.

Many investors do not accept the fact that the stock market represents corporate profits. Fear and greed determine that the stock market is irrational in the short term. But viewing the stock market as a collection of businesses benefits you in accumulating wealth. When corporate profits diverge from stock prices, that is your opportunity to become wealthy. The stock market after the “9/11” event is exactly opposite to the stock market at the end of the 1990s. Although stock prices plummeted like soccer-ball sized hail, corporate profits were hardly affected.

When the “stock market big sale” happens, rush to buy!
