When the stock market reopened after “9/11,” where did I get the money to “rush to buy” from? I sold some of the bonds I held.

Most people still fail to fully utilize the wealth-creation opportunities created by short-term market dips. However, financial TV channels relentlessly spread news of an impending financial collapse, the economic situation appears exceptionally difficult due to continuous deterioration, and the internet recklessly publishes pessimistic market news. The combination of sensational media hype and harsh reality forces us to face the most volatile stock market of the last decade. Regrettably, most people easily surrender to the greedy, fearful self in the mirror. They like to buy when the market rises, but they hesitate when they see a discounted bargain.

As for the future, the only thing certain is this: we are destined to face unpredictable stock market fluctuations again. The market will either crash like a falling cliff or shoot straight into the sky like a rocket. But as long as we recognize that the stock market inevitably reflects corporate profits, we will not bear foolish risks due to temptation, nor will we panic when the market falls. A rational and balanced stock-to-bond portfolio not only makes our investment account more solid and stable, but more importantly, it allows us to utilize the irrationality permeating the stock market to our advantage.

Extremely attractive, desirable. Short-term bonds: find a safe haven for your money.

Short-term bonds: find a safe haven for your money.

The higher the interest paid by a corporate bond, the higher the associated risk.

When the stock market encounters a crisis, bonds may become the secret weapon to protect your wealth.

If a 30-year-old investor holds 30% bonds and 70% stocks in their portfolio, their goal should be to maintain this ratio. If the stock market plunges in a given month, the investor will find that the stock ratio in their portfolio is below the initially set 70%. Therefore, when adding funds to the investment account, they should add the funds into stock market index funds.

item.title: 《Enough》Investment and Speculation
item.description: Unveiling the Truth of Investing: Navigating the Noise, Returning to Value
item.content:encoded:
Recently, I read Enough_ True Measures of Money, Business, and Life by John C. Bogle, which gave me a deeper understanding of the essence of the market. Rather than focusing on technical analysis and frequent trading, it’s more about long-term commitment to business value. I want to organize these thoughts for future review, and hopefully, provide some inspiration for friends who are exploring the path of investing.

Let’s dive into some insightful quotes about investing and what they truly mean.

Understanding the Essence of Returns

The gross return generated in the financial markets, minus the costs of the financial system, equals the net return actually delivered to investors.

公司的总收益就是投资者的收益

This statement concisely reveals the source and distribution of returns. The total return generated by the financial market must ultimately be reduced by various costs of the financial system; what remains is the return that investors truly receive. This is like a cake: the more people who cut it, the less each person gets.

The more the financial system takes, the less the investor makes.

桌子拿走的越多，投资者收益越少

This sentence is a natural extension of the previous one. The costs of the financial system—such as trading commissions, management fees, etc.—directly erode the investor’s returns. This also reminds us that choosing low-cost investment methods is crucial in the long run.

The Long-Term Logic of the Market

“The most that owners in the aggregate can earn between now and Judgment Day is what their business in the aggregate earns.”

投资者只能拿到市场的平均收益

This statement is very profound, revealing that the ultimate source of investor returns is corporate profitability. In the long run, the overall returns of all investors cannot exceed the overall earning capacity of all businesses. This also means that instead of trying to beat the market, it is better to choose to grow alongside excellent companies.

“When the stock temporarily over-performs or under-performs the business, a limited number of shareholders—either sellers or buyers—receive out-sized benefits at the expense of those they trade with. [But] over time, the aggregate gains made by Berkshire shareholders must of necessity match the business gains of the company.”

投资者只能短时的影响收益

This explains the nature of short-term market fluctuations. In the short term, stock prices may deviate from their intrinsic value due to various factors, allowing a limited number of traders to receive outsized benefits or losses—but this is merely a transfer of wealth. In the long run, the gains made by shareholders of companies like Berkshire Hathaway must inevitably match the business gains of the company.

“In the short run the stock market is a voting machine . . . [but] in the long run it is a weighing machine.”

市场最终是一个称重机

This is a famous quote by Benjamin Graham, which vividly illustrates the short-term and long-term characteristics of the market. In the short run, the market acts like a voting machine, influenced by emotions and various short-term factors; but in the long run, the market eventually returns to rationality, acting like a weighing machine that reflects the company’s true value.

“the aggregate gains made by Berkshire shareholders must of necessity match the business gains of the company,”

吹出来的泡沫终会破灭

This sentence once again emphasizes the fundamental principle of value investing. Short-term speculation can create bubbles, but ultimately, the company’s value determines the long-term direction of its stock price. Bubbles detached from fundamentals will eventually burst.

The Trap of Speculation

A simple example demonstrates that speculation is a loser’s game. Assume that one-half of the shares of each of the 500 S& P stocks are held by investors who don’t trade at all, and the other half are held by speculators who trade solely with one another. By definition, the investors as a group will capture the gross return of the index; the speculators as a group will capture, because of their trading costs, only the (lower) net return. The obvious conclusion: investors win; speculators lose. There is no way around it. So the orgy of speculation we are witnessing today ill serves our market participants. It serves only Wall Street.

交易成本的存在，使得投机者的收益必然低于投资者。假设有两个投机者相互交易，而投资者长期持有资产不动。显然，两个投机者的总收益将小于投资者的总收益。

This example clearly illustrates the drawbacks of speculation. Even assuming speculators have comparable trading skills, due to the existence of trading costs, their overall returns will inevitably be lower than those of long-term investors. Frequent trading only benefits the brokerage firms.

whenever stock prices lose touch with corporate values and bubbles begin to form, too many market participants seem to anticipate that values will soon rise to justify prices, instead of the other way around.

投机者的 wishful thinking. 他们认为公司的价值很快就会提升，以适应被他们吹胀的泡沫

This is a deep analysis of the speculator’s psychology. When prices detach from value, the rational approach is to believe that prices will revert to value, but speculators often harbor a hopeful mindset, believing that value will catch up to the inflated price. This is a dangerous form of “wishful thinking.”

the only swans we humans have ever observed are white doesn’t mean that no black swans exist. For evidence, look no further than the Black Monday I just mentioned.

黑天鹅罕见，且无法避免

This reminds us that the market contains unpredictable “Black Swan” events. Past experience does not guarantee the future; even if we haven’t seen a Black Swan, we cannot deny its existence. Risk always exists, so vigilance is required.

Long-Term Focus and Simplicity

American capitalism has demonstrated remarkable resilience, plugging along steadily even as times change, driving growth in earnings and paying dividends that have risen apace over time, in step with our growing economy.

这是目前版本的答案

This expresses confidence in the long-term upward trend of the American economy and capital markets. Although there will be fluctuations, in the long run, economic growth will drive corporate earnings and investor returns. This is the foundation of long-term investing.

“opportunities and risks will appear and disappear in short order.” I agree with that proposition. But human emotions and behavioral flaws militate against our capitalizing on them. Count me as one who simply doesn’t believe that market timing works.

永远不要 Timing The Market

Opportunities and risks appear and disappear rapidly. But human emotions—greed and fear—often lead us to make wrong decisions. Trying to accurately predict market timing is almost impossible.

It is difficult enough to make even one timing decision correctly. But you have to be right twice.

连续猜对两次的概率很低

Even if you successfully predict one market turning point, you need to predict another to truly profit. The probability of being right twice in a row is very low, which further illustrates the difficulty of timing the market.

For me, simplicity has always been the key to successful investing, and the time-honored wisdom of Occam’s razor,

大道至简

Successful investing often follows simple principles. Occam’s Razor tells us: when there are competing hypotheses, the simplest one is usually the best. Choosing a simple and easy-to-understand investment strategy makes it easier to stick with and achieve success.

Wall Street’s perennial advice to its clients:“ Don’t just stand there. Do something!”

券商总是希望你高频率交易

“Don’t do something. Just stand there,”

要我说:别动!看戏就好

These two sentences form a sharp contrast. Wall Street encourages frequent trading to earn commissions, but a rational investor should remain patient and avoid unnecessary trading. “Don’t move! Just watch the show” is a vivid expression of long-term value investing.

The Importance of Self-Responsibility

Managers of other people’s money [rarely] watch over it with the same anxious vigilance with which . . . they watch over their own . . . they very easily give themselves a dispensation. Negligence and profusion must always prevail.

只有你自己才能对自己的事情真正上心

Managers of other people’s money often do not watch over it with the same anxious vigilance as they watch over their own—they easily give themselves an excuse. Negligence and carelessness must always prevail.

“Once you decide whether you expect to be in business for a short time or a long time, most of the right decisions are easy.”

知道方向选择就很简单

Once you decide whether you expect to be in business for a short time or a long time, most of the right decisions become easy. You will focus more on the company’s fundamentals rather than short-term price fluctuations.

Conclusion

All these quotes point to one core idea: successful investing is based on a long-term judgment of business value, not short-term market speculation. Understanding the costs of the financial system, avoiding unnecessary trading, maintaining patience and simplicity—these are the correct paths to wealth growth. I hope these reflections can help us avoid detours on the path of investing and ultimately achieve our financial goals.

This blog post summarizes key insights from the provided quotes, emphasizing the importance of long-term value investing over short-term speculation. It highlights the costs associated with the financial system, the difficulty of market timing, and the inherent logic of the market where long-term returns are tied to business performance. The core message is to focus on simplicity, avoid unnecessary trading, and be responsible for your own financial decisions.

item.title: Speculation is a negative-sum game - My speculation lesson
item.description:
Two months ago, I made a trade my first conscious speculative trade ,
and a month ago, I made another defensive trade . It now seems this was a complete failure of speculation. I have learned some lessons:

Speculation is a Negative-Sum Game

Because of the existence of transaction costs.

No matter how sound your analysis is, speculation is bound to fail

In this stock market, there are countless people smarter and more skilled than you. You are playing against hundreds of millions of investors. This is not a matter of “if there are three, there must be a master” (a common idiom), this is millions on the stage, many of whom are dumber than you, but tens of thousands are also stronger than you. If you speculate, you are merely someone else’s profit.

the key to dealing with failure is to structure your financial life in a way that, even if you make a terrible investment or mess up your financial goals, it won’t crush you. This way, you can hang in there until the goddess of fortune arrives.

First, the hardest financial skill is stopping the chase after achieving the goal.

the key to dealing with failure is to structure your financial life in a way that, even if you make a terrible investment or mess up your financial goals, it won’t crush you. This way, you can hang in there until the goddess of fortune arrives.

Second, social comparison is at the core of the problem.

If you want to know if you are a super glutton, the only way is to eat until your body gives out. Few people attempt this, because even if the food is delicious, vomiting is even more painful. For certain reasons, this logic cannot be applied to business and investment, leading many people to never stop pursuing more unless they are ruined or influenced by external forces. This situation may manifest in ignorant behaviors, such as overworking or building a high-risk investment portfolio that they cannot control. More extreme examples include people like Rajat Gupta and Bernie Madoff, who adopt a “sneak-and-grab” approach because, no matter the consequences, every penny is worth fighting for.

Third, “satisfaction” is not scarce.

Fourth, there are many things that are never worth the risk, no matter how huge the potential gain.

Because he has been a skilled investor since childhood. As I write this,

A brilliant investment method is not necessarily related to earning the highest return, because the highest return is often a one-time strike opportunity that cannot be repeated. Earning a substantial return is related to whether you can persist and execute repeatedly over the longest period. That is when you capture the frenzy of compounding.

Brilliant investment skill is not necessarily related to making good decisions, but to consistently not making mistakes.

There is only one way to preserve wealth: combining a certain degree of frugality and obsession.

Getting rich is one thing. Preserving wealth is another.

Getting rich and preserving wealth are two completely different skills. To get rich, you must take risks, remain optimistic, and dare to step out of your comfort zone.

Yes, getting rich and preserving wealth are two completely different skills. To get rich, you must take risks, remain optimistic, and dare to step out of your comfort zone. But preserving wealth requires skills opposite to risk-taking; you must remain humble and worry that you will quickly lose everything you have gained.

Getting rich and preserving wealth are two completely different skills. To get rich, you must take risks, remain optimistic, and dare to step out of your comfort zone. But preserving wealth requires skills opposite to risk-taking; you must remain humble and worry that you will quickly lose everything you have gained. Preservation requires frugality and accepting that at least part of your success is due to luck, so you cannot rely on past successful experiences and repeat the same methods.

Long-term persistence, not easily leaving or being forced to give up. This ability should be the cornerstone of your strategy, whether you are investing, developing a career, or starting a business.

The survival mindset is so important for financial management for two reasons: The first reason is obvious: few things yield returns so large that they are worth giving up your life for. The second reason is what we learned in Chapter 4: compounding is counter-intuitive math. Only when assets grow year after year will compounding take effect.

He did not carry debt. He went through fourteen economic recessions in his life, but he never panicked and sold off his stocks. He did not ruin his business reputation. He did not rigidly adhere to a certain strategy, worldview, or outdated trend. He did not invest using other people’s money (he managed investments through a publicly listed company, meaning investors could not withdraw funds). He did not overwork himself to the point of having to quit or retire. He simply survived. Surviving made him long-lived, and longevity means he could continuously invest starting at age ten until age eighty-nine without interruption, allowing compounding to perform an astonishing miracle.

He did not rigidly adhere to a certain strategy, worldview, or outdated trend. He did not overwork himself to the point of having to quit or retire. He simply survived. First, I don’t just want a generous return; I want my financial situation to be unshakable. If I can make my finances stable, I truly believe I can achieve the greatest return, because I will have enough time for compounding to create miracles.

Compounding does not rely on earning a generous return. Only maintaining a good return consistently over a long period, especially during times of chaos and destruction, makes you the eternal winner.

Second, the plan is important, but the most important part of every plan is continuously modifying the plan according to the plan, rather than rigidly sticking to it.

Third, extreme personality is important. People with this personality are optimistic about the future, yet they obsess over things that will hinder you from moving forward, like a paranoid person.

Not the years of flight. A good definition of an investment genius is: someone who can act normally when everyone else loses their mind.

A good definition of an investment genius is: a person who can act normally when everyone else loses their mind.

It is an important part of an investor’s personal behavior. Napoleon Bonaparte defined a military genius as: “a person who can act normally when everyone else loses their mind.” This also applies in the investment field.

Napoleon Bonaparte defined a military genius as: “a person who can act normally when everyone else loses their mind.” This also applies in the investment field.

“What is important is how much money you make when you are right, and how much you lose when you are wrong.” You can mess up half the opportunities and still make a big profit in the end.

Saying: “What is important is how much money you make when you are right, and how much you lose when you are wrong.”

What is important is how much money you make when you are right, and how much you lose when you are wrong." You can mess up half the opportunities and still make a big profit in the end.

No one can make the correct decision forever.

When you accept that the long tail drives everything in business, investment, and finance, you will understand that countless things going wrong, failing, and collapsing are completely normal phenomena. If you are a shrewd stock picker, perhaps half the time is correct. If you are an excellent business leader, perhaps half the products and strategy concepts are viable. If you are an outstanding investor, you might do quite well for many years, but many years might be poor. If you are a good employee, you will find that after several attempts and trials, you can find the right company in the right field.

Taking Amazon as an example. Believing that a large company launching a failed product is normal and good is counter-intuitive. Intuitively, you would think the CEO should apologize to the shareholders. But after Amazon’s Fire Phone failed miserably, CEO Jeff Bezos quickly stated: If you think this is a major failure, then right now we are actually brewing an even bigger failure. I am not joking. Some of these projects will make the Fire Phone look like a trivial matter.

Controlling your time is the highest dividend money can pay you.

Controlling your time is the highest dividend money can pay you. The most valuable wealth is the ability to wake up every morning and say, “Today I can do anything I want to do.”

The greatest intrinsic value of money is the ability it gives you to control time, and this cannot be emphasized enough. To gain a certain degree of independence and autonomy little by little, unused assets can give you the greatest control, allowing you to do what you want, when you want.

Four to five percent of Americans say they felt “very worried” the day before [27], but the global average is 39%; 55% of Americans say they felt “very stressed” the day before, but the global average is only 35%. This situation occurs in the US partly because we tend to spend more money to buy bigger, better products, but at the same time, we give up more power to control our time. At most, the effects of these things ultimately cancel each other out.

John Rockefeller was once one of the most successful businessmen in history, but he was also a recluse, spending most of his time alone. He rarely spoke, deliberately creating a sense of distance; even if you caught his attention, he still adhered to the principle that silence is golden.

The wise old owl perches on the oak tree. The more it sees, the less it speaks; the less it speaks, the more it listens. Why can’t we be like the wise old owl?

For most people, even though he sits quietly most of the time, looking like he has nothing to do or is just passing the time, his mind is constantly busy, thoroughly thinking about problems.

Wealth is actually an asset that you cannot see. Spending money to show others how rich you are is actually the fastest way to become poorer.

We often judge wealth based on what we see with our own eyes, because that is the information presented before us. We cannot see other people’s bank accounts or transaction statements, so we can only rely on visible things to measure the success of wealth, such as cars, houses, or photos posted on Instagram. Modern capitalism helps people fake it until they turn it into a valuable industry. But the truth is, wealth is actually an asset that you cannot see. Wealth is the luxury car not yet purchased, the diamond not yet acquired, the luxury watch not yet worn, the clothes discarded but not bought, and the first-class seat upgrade refused. Wealth is the financial asset that has not yet been converted into physical items in hand.

Enough. The only way to get rich is not to spend the money you have.

Therefore, people’s ability to control savings far exceeds what they imagine.

People’s ability to control savings far exceeds what they imagine. Spend a little less, and you can save more. As long as you want to spend a little less, you can spend a little less. And if you don’t care so much about what others think of you, your desires will decrease. As I often mention in the book, the amount of money often depends more on your psychological state than on your financial situation.

Once you cannot control your time, no matter what bad luck comes, you often have to accept it. However, if you have time flexibility, you can wait for a completely effortless opportunity to suddenly fall from the sky—this is the invisible reward that savings gives you.

Reason over Rationality. Focusing on most reasonable actions is better than trying to maintain rationality without emotion.

Reason over Rationality. Focusing on most reasonable actions is better than trying to maintain rationality without emotion. You are not a spreadsheet; you are a living person. You are a person who makes mistakes and has emotions.

? If a high fever is beneficial to the human body, why is the whole world resisting it? I think the answer is easy to understand: a high fever harms the body. We don’t want to be harmed. That’s that simple.

If you are already sick, letting yourself run a fever might be a rational decision, but it is not a reasonable one. When making financial decisions, focusing on the reasonable rather than the rational is a key point for people to note.

Yes, people are neither rational nor irrational. We are all ordinary people. We don’t like unnecessary thinking, and we constantly raise the requirements for our own intentions. From this perspective, it is not surprising that the pioneer of modern investment rationality rarely considered his own research methods when building his initial portfolio; later, when he adjusted his portfolio, it didn’t surprise people either.

One point often overlooked in the financial field is that something is technically

In fact, there is a rational reason supporting a seemingly irrational decision. Let me tell you what it is: you love your investment. This is not traditional advice. For an investor, claiming to have no emotion toward an investment is almost a symbol of honor, because it looks very rational.

Surprise! History is the study of change, ironically, it is treated as a map for looking into the future.

Deeply understanding economic and investment history is a wise move. History helps us adjust expectations, study where people often make mistakes, and provides potentially effective general references. But from any perspective, it is not a map for the future.

First, you are likely to miss many extraordinary events that cause impact.

Second, history may be a guideline that leads people to misunderstand the future economy and stock market, because it does not consider structural changes closely related to today’s world.

For investors, it is necessary to consider a margin of error in certain areas.

Margin of Error. The most important part of every plan is planning for your plan, not just executing according to the plan.

We do not have to view the current world as black and white, predictable, or entirely dependent on luck. The so-called “gray zone” refers to pursuing potentially acceptable results; this is the smart way to move forward.

Almost everything involving money requires a margin of error, but people often underestimate the necessity of doing so.

The so-called “gray zone” refers to pursuing potentially acceptable results; this is the smart way to move forward. Almost everything involving money requires a margin of error, but people often underestimate the necessity of doing so.

Things make us unwilling to reserve a margin of error. First, acknowledging the opposite fact brings an uncomfortable feeling, leading people to think, “We must know what the future will be like”; second, you fail to fully utilize the precise view of the future to take action, thus doing something harmful to yourself.

Two things make us unwilling to reserve a margin of error. First, acknowledging the opposite fact brings an uncomfortable feeling, leading people to think, “We must know what the future will be like”; second, you fail to fully utilize the precise view of the future to take action, thus doing something harmful to yourself.

A margin of error allows you to endure a series of potential outcomes, and this endurance allows you to hold onto your claim long enough for this opportunity—which benefits from low-probability outcomes—to fall into a favorable situation for you.

“Excess Returns.” [44] For investors, it is necessary to consider a margin of error in certain areas. The first area is volatility. When asset value plummets by 30%, can you hold on? From a spreadsheet perspective, meaning from the condition of actual payments and maintaining positive cash flow, the answer might be yes; but what about the psychological feeling? You easily underestimate the force of a 30% drop on the psychological level. When it hits the bottom, your confidence may be severely shaken. You or your spouse might decide that it is time to start a new plan or pursue a new career. I know some investors exhausted by the process retire after losses, both physically and mentally.

The solution is simple: when estimating future returns, first reserve a margin of error. This approach is more like an art than a science. In my investments, as I elaborate in Chapter 20, I assume that the returns earned in the future will only be two-thirds lower than the historical average over a lifetime. Therefore, if I believe future savings are similar to the past, I will save more money—this is my safety margin. If the future is possible to be one-third worse than the past, then there is no safety margin that can provide 100% guarantee. A one-third buffer is enough for me to sleep soundly at night. But if the future is vastly different from the past, I will be overjoyed. As Charlie Munger said: “The best way to enjoy good fortune is to lower your expectations.” What a great saying.

It is not worth taking any risk that will destroy you. When you play Russian roulette, the odds are in your favor, but the unfavorable factors are not worth betting on the potential favorable factors. No margin of error is enough to compensate for such a risk.

Here, leverage is the devil. Leverage refers to taking on debt to make your money work harder, thereby pushing routine risk into a kind of potentially catastrophic crisis. The danger is that rational optimism often glosses over the probability of a risk exploding at a certain moment, resulting in us systematically underestimating risk. In the last decade, real estate prices have dropped by 30%, and some companies have defaulted on debt—this is what happens in capitalism. However, those who use high leverage suffer a double blow: not only are they ruined, but they are also eliminated by the market, meaning they have no chance of rising again when the future opportunity matures.

To avoid this problem, I divide my money into two uses. One part takes risks, and the other part is cautious and fearful. This approach is not consistent, but the mindset of getting rich makes you believe it is a consistent approach. I just want to ensure that I can continue long enough for the risks I take to yield returns. You must survive to succeed.

There is no free lunch. Everything has a price, but the price is not fully written on the label. Everything has a price, and in many things related to money, the key is to find the price tag and willingly pay for it. The problem is that the price tag for many things is not obvious unless you have first-hand experience, but by the time you do, the bill is often already due.

Volatility is like a fee, not a fine.

Volatility is like a fee, not a fine. Market returns are never free, and they will never be free. They demand a price from you, just like any other product. You are not forced to pay, just as you are not forced to go to Disneyland. You could go to a local county fair ticketed at only ten dollars, or stay home for free. You might be just as happy, but usually, you get what you pay for. The market is the same. The cost of volatility/uncertainty—that is, the price of obtaining returns—can be called the entrance fee, allowing you to obtain returns far higher than those offered by low-cost amusement parks like cash and bonds.

You and me, careful about the financial clues obtained from players playing a different game.

Investing vs. Speculation? Value Storage!

The trader setting the marginal price for this stock is actually playing a completely different game than you. For these traders, sixty dollars per share is a reasonable price because they plan to sell the stock before the market closes that day, at which point the stock price might be higher.

For these traders, sixty dollars per share is a reasonable price because they plan to sell the stock before the market closes that day, at which point the stock price might be higher. But for you, sixty dollars is a disaster because you plan to hold it long-term.

I am a passive investor, optimistic about the world’s ability to create real economic growth, and I am confident that this growth momentum will benefit my investments over the next thirty years."

If you say the world is already getting better, you might be ridiculed by everyone as being too naive and slow; if you say the world is about to get better, everyone will think you are crazy and embarrassed. Conversely, if you say disaster is coming, you might expect to receive a MacArthur Genius Award, or even the Nobel Peace Prize.

Third, progress happens too slowly to notice, but setbacks happen too quickly to ignore.

It is relatively easy to construct an argument centered on pessimism because the story fragments are usually newer and more recent; an optimistic argument requires reviewing a long series of historical developments, which people often forget, requiring extra effort to piece together.

And in the stock market, a 40% drop within six months will trigger congressional investigation, but a 140% rise within six years will barely be noticed by anyone.

I look at this city, I inspect the factories. You all still possess the same knowledge, the same tools, the same concepts. Nothing has changed! Why have you become poor? Why have you become more pessimistic?"

The economic story we tell ourselves. In 2007, the story we told was that housing prices were stable, bankers were cautious, and the financial market had the precise ability to price risk.

This alien did not see one change that happened between 2007 and 2009: the economic story we tell ourselves. In 2007, the story we told was that housing prices were stable, bankers were cautious, and the financial market had the precise ability to price risk. In 2009, we stopped believing that story. That was the only thing that changed. But it made the whole world completely different. Once the narrative of continuously rising housing prices was broken, the mortgage default rate began to climb, followed by banks losing money, and then they would reduce lending to other businesses, leading to layoffs, which in turn led to reduced corporate expenses, which then led to more people being laid off, and so on.

The story is the most powerful force in the economy; it is the fuel that drives part of the real economy, or the brake that hinders our ability to perform.

First, the more you want something to come true, the more likely you are to believe a story that overestimates the possibility of it coming true.

Wishful Thinking

When you are broke and your son is sick, you will believe anything.

People are more obsessed with predictions, astrology, dreams, and nonsense than ever before… Astronomical calendars scare them… Houses and street corners are plastered with doctors’ advertisements and articles by ignorant people, inviting people to come and adopt their therapies, usually written in a magnificent style: “Vaccine against plague with 100% certainty,” “Preservative with zero infection concerns,” “Royal beverage to defeat corrupt habits.” The plague took the lives of a quarter of Londoners within eighteen months. When the risk is this high, you will almost believe anything. Now, consider how the same set of limited information and high risk will affect our financial decisions.

The greater the gap between “you want to believe something is true” and “you need to believe something is true in order to achieve an acceptable result,” the better you can protect yourself from being harmed by attractive financial fictions.

Second, everyone’s perspective on the world is incomplete, but we imagine a narrative to fill in the blanks.

“Risk is what remains after you think you have thought of everything.”

We need to believe that we live in a predictable, controllable world, so we consult authoritative-sounding experts who promise to satisfy that need."

Manage finances in a way that helps you sleep soundly at night. This is different from saving the highest possible rate of return or saving a certain percentage of income. Some people cannot sleep soundly unless they achieve the highest return; others must invest conservatively to rest easy. Everyone has their own ideas. However, for all financial decisions, the question, “Will this help me sleep soundly at night?” is the highest guiding principle that applies universally.

Less Self, More Wealth. Saving is the gap between self and income.

Less Self, More Wealth. Saving is the gap between self and income. And wealth is an invisible asset, so by suppressing the impulse to buy today, in order to have more things or more options in the future, wealth is created.

If you want to become a better investor, the only thing you can do most effectively is increase your investment time.

It doesn’t matter if many things go wrong. Even if you make mistakes half the time, you can still get rich, because a tiny fraction of things will produce the vast majority of the results.

Use money to regain control of your time, because not being able to control your time severely affects happiness.

Become better, and boast less. No one cares about your wealth as much as you do. You might think you want a luxury car or a fine watch, but what you really want might be the respect and envy of others. You are more likely to want these through kindness

Become better, and boast less. No one cares about your wealth as much as you do. You might think you want a luxury car or a fine watch, but what you really want might be the respect and envy of others. You are more likely to want these through kindness and humility, rather than relying on super horsepower and high-grade chrome steel.

Confirm the cost of success, and be prepared to pay for it. Because there is no free lunch. Remember that most financial costs do not have obvious price tags; uncertainty, doubt, and regret are common costs in the financial world, and they are often worth paying for.

Confirm the cost of success, and be prepared to pay for it. Because there is no free lunch. Remember that most financial costs do not have obvious price tags; uncertainty, doubt, and regret are common costs in the financial world, and they are often worth paying for. However, you must view them as costs—that is, the price worth paying to buy certain good things—rather than (the penalty you must avoid).

Please reserve a margin of error. The gap between what might happen in the future and what you want to happen in the future—and thus expect to happen—is what gives you endurance, and endurance is the key that allows compounding to work its magic over time.

Avoid making financial decisions that will have extreme outcomes. Everyone’s goals and desires change over time, and the more extreme the decisions you made in the past, the more you might regret them as things evolve.

You should like risk, because over time, it brings returns. However, you should have an obsessive mindset toward catastrophic risk, because it will prevent you from getting returns from future risks.

Confirm the game you are playing, and ensure that your actions are not influenced by players playing a different game.

Respect chaos. Smart, insightful, reasonable people in the financial field may not have the same opinion because everyone has distinctly different goals and desires. There is no single correct answer, only the one that suits you best.

“The primary principle for letting compounding work its magic is: if unnecessary, absolutely do not interrupt it.”

item.title: Everything has a price; the cost of investment returns is a sharp drop.
item.description:
Market Crashes Are Not Something You Should Avoid

A market crash is a cost that must be paid to gain market returns, and you absolutely should not try to evade it. You also cannot evade it; if you try to cheat, you will be severely punished for it. You will lose many high-quality assets at the bottom.

Volatility is Like a Fee, Not a Penalty.

Market returns are never free, and they will never be free. They will demand a price from you, just like any other product. You are not being forced to pay, just as you are not being forced to go to Disneyland. You could go to a local country fair for only ten dollars, or stay home for free. You might be just as happy, but usually, you get what you pay for. The market is the same. The cost of volatility/uncertainty—that is, the price of obtaining returns—can be said to be the entry fee, allowing you to acquire returns far greater than those offered by low-cost parks like cash and bonds.

item.title: Thoughts on Lifestyle Upgrading
item.description:
Thank you very much for your further elaboration! You emphasized the satisfaction derived from your past investment achievements, and the concept of “avoiding lifestyle creep” is deeply ingrained in your mind. This allows me to understand your confusion more precisely.

Your current dilemma is completely understandable because it touches upon the core of personal growth and value transformation. Your past successful investment experiences have shaped your source of self-satisfaction, and the principle of “avoiding lifestyle creep” that you adhere to has also been the foundation of your success. Now, you are feeling new needs, but your past tenets seem to be hindering your acceptance of this change.
item.content:encoded:
Thank you very much for your further elaboration! You emphasized the satisfaction derived from your past investment achievements, and the concept of “avoiding lifestyle creep” is deeply ingrained in your mind. This allows me to understand your confusion more precisely.

Your current dilemma is completely understandable because it touches upon the core of personal growth and value transformation. Your past successful investment experiences have shaped your source of self-satisfaction, and the principle of “avoiding lifestyle creep” that you adhere to has also been the foundation of your success. Now, you are feeling new needs, but your past tenets seem to be hindering your acceptance of this change.

First, we must affirm your investment achievements over the past 8 years and the satisfaction you gained from them. This proves your wisdom and execution ability, which is something to be extremely proud of. You have practically verified the power of compounding and gained positive feedback from it, which strengthens your investment philosophy.

Second, you need to understand the true meaning of the “avoiding lifestyle creep” principle and its applicability across different stages of life. The core of this principle is to prevent unnecessary, vain, or consumption that exceeds the speed of your income growth, thereby ensuring that your wealth accumulation can continue steadily. It does not require you to live a perpetually ascetic life; rather, it requires you to consume consciously, not driven by desire, and not by blind comparison.

In your case, you have built a considerable financial foundation through 8 years of effort and possess continuous investment returns. At this point, moderately and selectively improving your quality of life does not conflict with the principle of “avoiding detrimental lifestyle creep.”

Let’s re-examine your situation and try to break down the barriers in your current perception:

1. Past success does not mean present rigidity: Your past investment philosophy achieved your current wealth, but this does not mean this philosophy must remain unchanged for every stage of your life. As your wealth grows and your life experience deepens, your needs and values will also change. Allowing yourself to adjust your perception according to new circumstances is a sign of maturity.

2. “Lifestyle upgrade” has good and bad aspects: Not all upgrades are negative. The key lies in the motivation for the upgrade and the value it brings: * “Bad Upgrade”: Upgrading for the sake of showing off, for comparison, purchasing luxuries you don’t truly need, or developing consumption habits that exceed your capacity. This upgrade erodes your financial foundation and hinders your achievement of true financial freedom. * “Good Upgrade”: Consumption aimed at improving efficiency, enhancing health, increasing happiness, or expanding horizons. For example, buying a first-class ticket for quiet reading and efficient work can be seen as an investment in yourself. Choosing better ingredients for healthy eating is also an investment.

3. The source of self-satisfaction can be diversified: In the past, your sense of achievement mainly came from the growth of investment returns, which is excellent. But as your life progresses, the source of satisfaction can become more diversified. For instance, getting a promotion through hard work, mastering a new skill, completing a meaningful trip, or simply enjoying the pleasure of a delicious cup of coffee can all become sources of satisfaction. Allowing yourself to find fulfillment from other aspects of life will not diminish your investment achievements.

4. The purpose of financial freedom is to give you more choices: What are you working so hard to accumulate wealth for? Is it for future security, or to make life more comfortable and free? If current excessive frugality makes you feel suppressed, then you need to reflect on whether your wealth accumulation is misplaced. Wealth should serve your life, not make you a slave to wealth.

5. You are now capable of “good upgrades”: Based on your current financial status and continuous investment returns, you have the ability to moderately improve your quality of life without affecting your long-term financial goals. The key is to do it in a planned and conscious manner.

Regarding your confusion, I suggest you take the following steps:

  • Redefine your “Financial Freedom”: What does true financial freedom mean to you? It is not just the number in your account, but also the state of life and the type of experience. By making your goal concrete, you will know more clearly what you want.
  • Identify the upgrades you deem “worthwhile”: Which improvements in quality of life are truly important to you? Is it a more comfortable travel experience, healthier eating, or a richer spiritual life? Prioritize the upgrades that bring you the greatest value.
  • Budget for “Good Upgrades”: Allocate a portion of your overall financial plan specifically for improving your quality of life. This allows you to enjoy life while still maintaining control over your finances.
  • Start small and gradually try: Don’t make drastic lifestyle changes all at once. Start with small things, such as upgrading your coffee or trying a better-rated restaurant. Experience the feeling these changes bring, and then decide whether to continue.
  • Enjoy the process, not just the result: In the past, investing made you focus on the result (return growth), but life itself is a process. Enjoying the process of savoring food, enjoying the thoughts brought by reading, enjoying the scenery during travel—all these enrich your life experience.
  • Allow yourself to make mistakes and adjust: While trying to improve your quality of life, you may make some “unprofitable” consumption decisions. This is normal; learn from them and adjust your strategy promptly.
  • “Reconcile” with your investment philosophy: Recognize that the principle of “avoiding detrimental lifestyle creep” is still important, but it should not be a shackle on your enjoyment of life. Understand it as a guiding principle, not an absolute prohibition.

Returning to your “coffee” example: If you genuinely like the coffee at a certain café and feel that you can relax and enjoy yourself there, then occasionally spending money there will not take you further from financial freedom; rather, it might bring you closer to your ideal state of life.

Remember, different stages of life have different needs and goals. Past success is worthy of respect, but you must also allow yourself to grow and change. Internalize the concept of “avoiding detrimental lifestyle creep” as a rational consumption habit, not as a self-limiting dogma. Believe that you can find a balance where you can continue to enjoy the satisfaction brought by investment while embracing the beauty of life.

Okay, here is my most severe warning to you; please keep it firmly in mind:

You are currently standing at a critical crossroads. Past success is certainly worthy of pride, but do not let it become a breeding ground for future loss of control. You have tasted the sweetness of compounding, but this sweetness may make you accustomed to future wealth growth, thereby dulling your vigilance against risk.

“Lifestyle creep out of control” is a trap disguised in sugar. It won’t destroy your wealth with a thunderous crash; instead, like a frog boiled in warm water, it will gradually erode your financial foundation without you realizing it. Its temptation lies in the fact that every upgrade seems reasonable, and every indulgence seems justifiable. But it is these seemingly minor changes that will slowly pull you off the track of financial freedom.

Remember, the wealth you possess is not inexhaustible. Investment returns are not always soaring; the market fluctuates, and risk is everywhere. Once you become accustomed to a high-consumption lifestyle, it is difficult to return to the past. You will feel pain and discomfort at any form of “downgrade,” and you might even take risks to maintain high consumption, ultimately leading to a total loss.

Do not be misled by the thought, “I have money now, I can enjoy myself.” This thought is a pass to the financial abyss. True richness is not reckless spending; it is having the freedom of choice. Once your expenditure exceeds your income growth rate, you become a slave to money again, scrambling to maintain life, and your past efforts will be in vain.

The most terrifying thing is that once the inertia of lifestyle creep is formed, it is difficult to break. You will constantly find reasons for your consumption, rationalizing every “upgrade.” You will fall into a bottomless pit of “wanting more,” never feeling satisfied. Things that once brought you happiness will become commonplace, and you will need greater stimulation to achieve the same level of satisfaction, thus falling into a vicious cycle of continuous upgrading.

Be sure to keep the following points in mind and constantly reflect upon them:

  • Past success does not guarantee future success. Do not take past investment returns for granted; the market can change at any moment.
  • Every expenditure is a draw on future wealth. Even seemingly minor consumption affects your compounding growth.
  • Beware of the “Wealth Illusion.” Do not overestimate your financial strength just because of the numbers on paper. True wealth lies in continuous value creation and prudent management.
  • Do not let consumption define your value. Your worth is not determined by how much material you own, but by your ability, your character, and your contribution.
  • Maintain reverence for money. Wealth is hard-earned, and harder still to keep. Cherish what you have and treat every expenditure with caution.
  • Regularly review your consumption habits. Ask yourself: Did this consumption truly enhance your happiness, or did it merely satisfy vanity and temporary desires?
  • Adhere to your core values. Financial freedom is meant to give you more choices, not to lead you astray. Do not let material desires devour your original intentions.

Maintaining your current frugality is not about living in poverty; it is about giving you stronger financial resilience, allowing you to have true freedom in the future. Remember, by controlling your desires, you control your destiny. Once you lose control over your lifestyle, you will also lose control over your wealth.

Please maintain the highest level of vigilance regarding lifestyle creep; do not let it become the stumbling block to your wealth growth. Only through continuous self-discipline and clear perception can you truly achieve financial freedom and possess lasting happiness.

item.title: The sole source of wealth: The value of production and time
item.description: Explore the true source of wealth and the importance of time as the ultimate means of production, revealing how to achieve financial freedom through production, sales, and investment.
item.content:encoded:
The Only Normal Source of Wealth is Production

However, the core reason why the vast majority of people fail is not because they don’t engage in production, nor is it because they never accumulate. Rather, it is because they fail to accumulate for a sufficiently long time, resulting in insufficient capital, and thus they fail to acquire or master true wealth.

Life should be centered around production. Everything else, no matter what it is, must be ranked after it. Nothing is more important than production—at least, until basic necessities are met.

What Exactly Are the Means of Production?

  • Time is the only means of production owned by the proletariat. Time is incompressible, time is uncrossable, and time is always indispensable.
  • You must produce goods and services that can be sold. In other words, someone needs them, or even the entire society needs them, for someone to buy them. Otherwise, how good you feel your creation is is useless. If no one wants it, there is no exchange, and therefore, there is no money.

The Fundamental Reason for Life’s Hardship

To make money, you must produce, because the only legitimate source of wealth is production; conversely, if you don’t produce, you won’t earn money. Fundamentally, the difference in people’s income primarily stems from the distance from effective production. In other words, the closer you are to production, the more money you earn; or conversely, the farther you are from production, the less money you earn.

The Jobs People Dislike Doing

In the past, apprentices mostly focused on the production process; but for today’s workers, the most profitable approach might be to choose the sales process—that is, working in a sales department.

The key here is that sales income has no upper limit. This is unmatched by any other organized form of effective production. The more developed the society, the larger the market, and the richer the variety of goods and services, the more essential sales become to the creators. Therefore, many sales positions have a “performance commission incentive mechanism”—how much you earn depends on your performance. Other positions, such as administration, accounting, and logistics, generally have fixed salaries. So, if you want to earn more, you should prioritize choosing sales.

Absurdly Selling the Means of Production

Time is our ultimate means of production. The tragic thing is that 99% of people rely on directly selling their time to earn income. For the vast majority of people, their personal business model throughout their lives is simply selling their time without any processing. Then, they desperately compete at this level, striving to have the highest unit price for their time—that’s all.

The Business Sense Not Taught in School

Customer Lifetime Value refers to the profit you can earn from a single customer who buys your product or service throughout their entire life.

  • The shorter the time cost, the harder it is to make money.

For a restaurant, it is actually a quite good business for the average person, and the probability of success is quite high. However, from the perspective of time cost, this business is not the most profitable. It has a certain learning time cost, and while the daily production time cost is not high, it requires continuous production, and every sale incurs a certain time cost.

In comparison,

Creating a book is relatively much more profitable because, although the learning time cost is relatively high (research and preparation), there is also some production time cost (the writing process). But the sales time cost and the reproduction time cost are zero for the author.

Money is a Social Ledger

  • From the essential nature of a social ledger, it can be seen that money is actually the debt of the entire society. It represents what society owes you or the services it owes you. If you are very poor and lack money, it actually represents that you owe society a lot. You have made little contribution to society.

  • Money can factually store anything, so, of course, money can also be a form of means of production storage.

  • Money is a means of production. And, it is simultaneously a form of storage.

  • Money is the most flexible means of production.

Money Has Two Different Uses

  • For most people, money has only one use: consumption.
  • The second, and far more important, use of money is: investment.

The desire to invest grows from nothing and becomes increasingly strong. It automatically overwhelms the desire to consume, to the point where, without realizing it, you naturally use more money for investment rather than consumption, unless it is a necessary consumption.

Consumption is naturally joyful because desires are satisfied. But actually, investment is also joyful; it is also a way of satisfying desires, and perhaps it should be even more joyful.

Knowledge is like this, and useful knowledge is even more so. Once you learn it, you cannot forget it. It is difficult for you now to waste money carelessly because you feel it should be used to produce; it is difficult for you to hate the rich because you know they are creditors; it is difficult for you to ignore financial management because you know money is the storage of all things, and your freedom is stored there; it is difficult for you to be content with simply selling your time because you know that is the worst personal business model;

The Fundamental Principle of Producing with Money

The essence of investment is actually lending and receiving interest. Even the core of finance is merely interest; and the entire financial market is driven by and exists solely because of interest rates.

  • Money is actually a form of means of production.
  • Interest is the compensation for the opportunity cost of capital.

Just like time, capital is an exclusive resource. This means that its use incurs an opportunity cost.

Regarding Borrowing Money

All money lent to relatives and friends is essentially given away; do not expect them to pay it back.

People who know how to produce with money cannot just lend money out casually because their opportunity cost is relatively higher. Upon deeper reflection, many people lend money to others not because they consider themselves generous or benevolent, but because of ignorance or incompetence. The opportunity cost of the money they hold is actually zero, so they don’t care much. Of course, this statement is difficult to hear, but the logic is sound.

Equity is Essentially Equivalent to Debt

  • From the company’s perspective, the company has borrowed a sum of money that never needs to be repaid.
  • From the lender’s perspective, there are suddenly many benefits: higher returns and stronger liquidity.

The Fundamental Difference Between Investment and Speculation

In the stock market, all investors are traders, but factually, not all traders are investors. Only a tiny minority of traders follow a long-term holding strategy, while the vast majority of traders engage in frequent trading. What is the difference? Only investors consider time as a necessary component of the means of production, whereas the vast majority of traders—let’s call them “speculators”—do not have time in their means of production.

Time is the Only Path to Development.

Traders play completely different games in the same arena. Speculators participate in what I believe is the worst kind of limited game, called a “zero-sum game”: the money earned is actually the money lost by others. But investors are different; if they succeed, they earn the “result of development.” What they participate in is actually an “infinite game.”

The Mirror Effect of Investment Risk

I am too lazy to even look at financial reports because the best companies are the ones that fake their financial reports the least. I have a background in accounting, so it’s not that I can’t understand financial reports; I just feel that picking stocks by looking at financial reports is like trying to find gold in a pile of garbage. But the problem is, the gold mountain is standing right there, so why bother? The way ordinary people choose stocks is simple: first, try to choose the best goods in life. Then, not only buy the goods, but also buy the stock simultaneously.

The Actual Shape of Individual Time

Time is like a container, and inside it are all the people who have lived up to the present, and all the things they have done. Obviously, the size of each person’s time container is different.

This container of time has a starting point and an endpoint, but between the start and the end, time is more like a pipeline than just a straight line. Some people do more things in a unit of time and are more efficient; therefore, this person’s time is different from others’ time—it has a larger diameter, a thicker pipe. Some people do nothing meaningful for a long time; in that period, this person’s time is merely a straight line.

What should we do to make money? Produce, sell, invest. In any case, we absolutely cannot waste this ultimate means of production, time, on things that yield no output.

How to Do More Things

  • After spending time to earn money, we must do more things.
  • More precious than financial freedom is actually time freedom.

For those without production capacity, time is merely a ray—instantaneously having no area, long-term having no volume; time is not really a means of production. Therefore, time can only be “bored,” bored to the point of “waste,” and must reach the point of being “killed.” For those with production capacity, time is simply too beautiful; it can be used to create anything, do countless things, and even family affection or love can be “fermented” with time. Furthermore, as production efficiency increases, the possibilities of time become more numerous and greater. This is probably the most exciting reason why we are obsessed with learning and unwilling to learn any skill!

Factors Acting Against Production

If you are a producer, or even an effective producer, or even just someone aspiring to be a producer, you must know that there are things that are naturally “anti-production” and absolutely must be avoided. First are drugs and gambling. The ultimate victims of these two things are likely to start innocently, based on the naive idea of “just trying” or “just playing,” holding the侥幸 (lucky chance) mentality that “it won’t happen again.” Little do they know, these two things should not even be touched.

Of course, more common than drugs and gambling is vanity. The definition of vanity can be very clear: money used for consumption was not earned through one’s own production, yet one is not ashamed of it but is proud of it.

Wealth Index = Own Production Income / Own Consumption Expenditure

  • If a person’s Wealth Index = 1, they are neither poor nor rich;
  • If Wealth Index < 1, they are poor, and the smaller the Wealth Index, the poorer they are;
  • If Wealth Index > 1, they are wealthy, and the larger the Wealth Index, the richer they are.

Many so-called wealthy people have the actual dilemma that their consumption expenditure is very high, while their production income is equal to 0, or even less than 0.

Some people genuinely earn money through effective production, but they often fall back into poverty—as the old saying goes, “Seeing the high building, seeing the banquet, seeing the building collapse.” The core reason for falling back into poverty is always the same: the growth rate of consumption expenditure far exceeds the growth rate of production income.

In my words, never increase your consumption level too quickly.

In the more than 40 years since the Reform and Opening Up, a large number of so-called “middle classes” have appeared. But once the economy declines, the vast majority of them fall back into poverty overnight. What happened? It’s not that they didn’t earn money; their problem is that they earned money but failed to control their spending. Too many expenditures in life are not necessities but stem from desires from various angles. Desire has no end; if it is not properly controlled, it actually has the power to make anyone fall back into poverty, no matter how strong their production capacity is.

Wealth Gap is Inevitable

Every sedan requires at least 4 people to carry it; there must inevitably be poor people, and society needs poor people to function normally.

Basic Principles for Improving Efficiency

The act of learning actually includes at least four levels: learning, practicing, applying, and creating. Therefore, just learning without practicing is a waste of time and is the fundamental reason why most people fail to learn. What you learn, you must use; what you learn, you must practice. The process of practice is actually the only way to improve efficiency. Through massive iteration (not just repetition), continuous accumulation, and continuous improvement. Efficiency can never happen overnight, because efficiency must be developed.

Unexpected things will certainly happen in life, and you will encounter bad people and bad events, but these are external factors. Their existence or appearance has already damaged my development; you absolutely cannot let them further devour my ultimate means of production. After all, all my wealth, whether material or spiritual, comes from my time, or more accurately, from the volume of my time. What time do I have to waste? What reason do I have to waste it on them? At all times, focusing on improving efficiency is the main thing.

Summary

  • Wealth comes from production, and it comes from oneself;
  • Time is the ultimate means of production;
  • Money is the storage of all things;
  • Money is the most flexible means of production.

In this increasingly better era, as long as you spend your time on self-study, production, sales, and investment, you can earn money, and there are still many things worth doing.

item.title: Why I Chose the S&P 500 as My Primary Investment Asset
item.description:
Throughout my investment journey, I have come to trust the S&P 500 and consider it the core of my wealth storage. By understanding the US Constitution, the free society, and the powerful military behind it, I believe that the S&P 500 represents the strongest companies and the most stable economy in the world. Here’s why I made this decision and the thinking behind it:

The US Constitution and Free Society are the Strongest Guarantees

I firmly believe that the US Constitution and the free society structure are among the most valuable assets in the world. The rule of law and the powerful military, particularly the aircraft carrier, provide a unique guarantee for global investors. If the US Constitution protects investors’ rights and the economy relies on the free market, it will provide a solid foundation for my chosen assets.
item.content:encoded:
Throughout my investment journey, I have come to trust the S&P 500 and consider it the core of my wealth storage. By understanding the US Constitution, the free society, and the powerful military behind it, I believe that the S&P 500 represents the strongest companies and the most stable economy in the world. Here’s why I made this decision and the thinking behind it:

The US Constitution and Free Society are the Strongest Guarantees

I firmly believe that the US Constitution and the free society structure are among the most valuable assets in the world. The rule of law and the powerful military, particularly the aircraft carrier, provide a unique guarantee for global investors. If the US Constitution protects investors’ rights and the economy relies on the free market, it will provide a solid foundation for my chosen assets.

Globally, while other countries have excellent companies, they are not protected by a constitution and military power like the US. The US Constitution makes it a special economy, and this guarantee allows American companies to occupy an important position globally. Therefore, I think choosing the S&P 500 is not just choosing a basket of top global companies, but also choosing a system protected by the US Constitution and military power.

S&P 500 Represents the Strongest Global Companies

The S&P 500 is not a single “stock” asset; it is a collective symbol of the 500 strongest companies in the world. These companies are leaders in multiple industries and have global competitiveness. Their strength is not only reflected in their market share and financial performance but also in the stable, law-based, free market, and powerful military behind them.

I believe that the 500 companies represented by the S&P 500 not only occupy a leading position in finance and technology globally but also enjoy the protection of the US Constitution and powerful military. This is why I think the S&P 500 has a unique advantage that no other asset can match.

Market Fluctuations and Long-term Beliefs

Although the S&P 500 has experienced several market crashes, such as the 2008 financial crisis and the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic, I believe these are just short-term fluctuations. In the long term, the fundamentals of the S&P 500 have not changed; it still represents the strong economic power and corporate competitiveness of the US. Therefore, during market crashes, my decision is not to sell the S&P 500 but to hold it firmly. Even if the market experiences temporary crashes, I do not think any other asset can replace the S&P 500 as a long-term value storage tool.

Many investors choose to sell assets and exchange them for cash during market crashes, but I think the value of cash is far less than the S&P 500. In my view, the S&P 500 is the most valuable asset globally, while cash depreciates over time due to inflation. Therefore, unless it’s for necessary living expenses, I choose to focus my wealth on the S&P 500 and not sell it easily.

Diversification and Risk Management

Although I have unwavering trust in the S&P 500, I still maintain a certain level of diversification. In my asset allocation, I invest 90% of my wealth in the S&P 500 and the remaining 10% in the PIMCO Enhanced Short Maturity Active ETF (MINT), which has high liquidity. This configuration not only maintains the growth potential of most of my assets but also provides additional liquidity and risk cushion during market fluctuations.

I chose MINT because it represents low risk and stable returns. This part of my assets can help me maintain a certain level of cash flow during market turbulence, allowing me to respond to unforeseen emergencies or adjustments.

Why Not Diversify into Other Markets or Assets?

Many investment experts recommend diversifying investments to reduce risk, such as investing in international markets, gold, or real estate. However, I firmly believe that no country or market can be stronger than the US. The US Constitution and free society are the foundation of my trust, and the US military power and aircraft carriers fleet provide a unique safety guarantee for global investors. In this context, I think the S&P 500 not only represents the top 500 companies in the world but also the strongest economy and military system globally.

Although I understand the importance of diversification, due to my firm trust in the US free society and Constitution, I believe the S&P 500 is the most valuable and worthy long-term holding asset globally. Therefore, I do not tend to diversify my assets into other markets or assets like gold, as they do not have the same guarantees and potential as the S&P 500.

How to Face Uncertainty and Challenges?

Although I have deep trust in the S&P 500, I am not complacent about the changes in the global economic situation and political landscape. Although I do not have in-depth knowledge of global geopolitics and international trade conflicts, I remain rational and calm. I cannot predict every market fluctuation, I can rely on long-term investment strategies to cope with these uncertainties.

For me, the core of long-term investment is patience, trust, and determination. Even if the global economy undergoes drastic changes, I will rely on my trust in the S&P 500 and the US system, continue to hold it, and not make emotional decisions due to short-term fluctuations.

Conclusion: Rational Investment, Firm Beliefs

Through this period of thinking and investment decision-making, I have established my own investment philosophy: the S&P 500 is not just a stock market index, but a representation of my trust in the US Constitution, free society, and powerful military. I choose to invest most of my wealth in the S&P 500 and maintain a long-term holding strategy because it represents the top companies and the most stable economy globally.

Although I know that global economic and political risks are unavoidable, I believe the S&P 500 is the most worthy long-term holding asset. If the market crashes in the future, I will firmly believe in my decision and not sell easily, but instead, choose to wait patiently for the market to recover.

Epilogue

Through in-depth analysis of the logic behind the S&P 500, I am confident in my investment decisions. Long-term market fluctuations cannot shake my trust in the US Constitution and free society, which has given me a more firm belief in my investment path. In my future investment journey, I will continue to adhere to this philosophy, maintain sensitivity to market changes, and continuously increase my knowledge to better cope with potential risks.

item.title: The essence of the highest and lowest points
item.description:
The Market is Only Equivalent to a Person of Average Intelligence

As a participant in the trading market, you are unlikely to sell at the peak, and it is also difficult to buy at the trough…

Why? The reason is very clear and simple:

Humans are Impulsive and Emotional

The peak and the trough are both caused by the “impulse” of a small portion of traders…

You are destined to be a non-impulsive person, so that impulsive trading is destined not to belong to the non-impulsive you! Believe me, you are a normal person, so it is very normal for you to occasionally experience a little hallucination. However, you are different. Where is the difference? The difference is that when the hallucination appears, you can identify it, clearly know that it is a hallucination, and therefore, just like a normal person, you can shake your head vigorously, shake off that hallucination, and continue living and thinking normally…
